speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: RIGHT HON. HAROLD HOLT EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON DEATH OF AUSTRALIAN PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure members of this house would expect me to express our feeling of shock and grief at the tragic accident that resulted in the loss of the prime minister of Australia over the week end.
Mr. Holt was a very distinguished Australian public servant over many years, culminating in his succession to Sir Robert Men-zies as prime minister only a relatively short time ago. In that post he had so much to offer and so little time in which to offer it. He was a very strong supporter of the commonwealth and a very good friend of Canada. I know from talks with him that he was most anxious to deepen and develop the friendship between our two countries, both as members of the commonwealth and as Pacific powers.
Mr. Holt will be greatly missed, of course, in his own country but also outside Australia. He was a man of energy, great enthusiasm and warm natural friendliness, qualities which we associate with Australians. He was a good and valued friend of many of us, including myself. I had the privilege of welcoming him to Ottawa officially last summer, and my wife and I had the privilege and pleasure of spending a day or so with him in the country. It was only last Friday, Mr. Speaker, that I received a message from him expressing the hope that my own plans would not prevent a visit to Australia and New Zealand which I was anticipating. He said he looked forward to receiving me as host and as friend.
Our deepest and most heartfelt sympathy goes out to his devoted and courageous wife, Mrs. Holt, and to the members of the family.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: RIGHT HON. HAROLD HOLT EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON DEATH OF AUSTRALIAN PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the comments made by the right hon. Prime Minister. It is very difficult to understand this sort of thing when
it happens. It is difficult to grasp that our sister commonwealth country, Australia, should lose its prime minister through such circumstances. Although Australia is a long distance from Canada I believe Canadians feel a particular cordiality and warmth to the people of Australia.
All Canadians suffered shock and a sense of loss when they heard or read about this tragic accident. I believe all the people of Canada would wish us to extend to the prime minister's family and indeed to the people of Australia our deepest sympathy on this very sad occasion.

maintopic: RIGHT HON. HAROLD HOLT EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON DEATH OF AUSTRALIAN PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we share with hon. members of this house the sorrow expressed over the untimely death of Right Hon. Harold Holt, the late prime minister of Australia. As has been mentioned, Mr. Holt has given many years of distinguished service to his country in both domestic and external affairs. His courage and leadership will be sorely missed at this time. We in this party join in the expressions of sympathy to his country, to Mrs. Holt and the members of the family in this hour of their sorrow and loss.

December 18, 1967
External Affairs EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of National Defence and I have just returned from attending the first ministerial meeting of the north Atlantic alliance council to be held at the new headquarters of NATO in Brussels. It seemed to both of us that in making a report to the house it would perhaps be prudent if I were to make a report in respect of the matters which involve me as Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence would make a report as well, and that if this is agreeable these would constitute the government report at this particular moment.
The speed and efficiency with which NATO was able to move to its new headquarters are a credit to the Belgian authorities and to the NATO international staff.
This was an important meeting. Indeed, I believe it may turn out to have been one of the key meetings in the history of the alliance. NATO has reappraised its essential objectives and found them still valid, agreed on a new military strategy, and established guide lines for shifting additional emphasis to its evolving political-as distinct from military-activity. The guide lines were the product of the so-called Harmel exercise. At our last meeting in Paris in 1966 the Belgian foreign minister, Mr. Harmel, recalling the initiative taken by Canada in 1964, had proposed a study of the future of the alliance. As a result of this serious reappraisal it was possible to reach a consensus among all 15 members on the objectives and future tasks of the alliance. This consensus is expressed in an annex to the communique, which I should be pleased to table if it is the desire of the house.
speakername: Hon. Paul  Marlin@Secretary of Slate for External Affairs

speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The member governments have confirmed that there is a continuing need for defensive military arrangements; I wish it were otherwise, but such arrangements are required, just as the regular payment of an insurance premium. In this field the alliance must display determination and firmness.
It was also confirmed that the activities of the alliance to promote a peaceful settlement, that is its political role, have assumed greater importance and should be emphasized. Here

is something which is partly new and challenging. In this field the alliance will require imagination and vision. It was affirmed that the political activities of the alliance will be all the more effective if there is full and timely consultation among the members. It was agreed that the military tasks of the alliance are not incompatible with, but rather a necessary complement to, a constructive political role for the alliance.
What does this1 signify for the alliance and for Canada? In the military sphere it means that as insurance against possible revived Soviet pressures in Europe, bearing in mind that Soviet military capabilities are still increasing, the alliance must maintain an effective deterrent force. For Canada, as a partner in the alliance, it means continuing to contribute, as appropriate, to the alliance's forces based in Europe and to those based in Canada.
On the political side the conclusions of the Harmel exercise mean that our habit of frank discussion among allies of the most important issues facing the alliance and the world, both collectively and individually, is to be further developed. Such consultations I believe are a powerful factor in promoting wider understanding of the issues facing the alliance, and in this way contributing to its cohesion.
The habit of co-operation and consultation in NATO fits it to perform a constructive role in many areas; balanced force reductions, arms control and disarmament measures, improvement of east-west relations, the shape and content of a European settlement and steps which may be taken toward negotiation of such a settlement.
We cannot expect instant or dramatic developments in these areas. There is much to be done, and it will be a painstaking and time consuming task to end the tensions in Europe and achieve a viable settlement. But much depends on the Russians as well as ourselves. It has been abundantly clear, for instance, that the alliance is prepared to explore mutual reductions of forces with the Soviet union and its allies as an important step toward security and stability. But there has been no indication as yet from the Russians, explicit or tacit, that they are ready to respond on this issue. But we must continue the search for agreement, and I can assure the house that Canada will be a vigorous participant in this search.
December 18, 1967

As I said at the conclusion of the ministerial meeting, NATO has confirmed and emphasized its determination to pursue what I think can be aptly described as a dynamic quest for peace. I can assure the house that the quest for peace will be as sustained and resourceful as we can make it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Leo Cadieux (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to report on the meetings of the nuclear defence affairs committee and the defence planning committee which preceded the meeting of the NATO council about which my hon. colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, has just spoken.
First I would like to deal with the meeting of the nuclear defence afftirs committee, which was established a year ago so that all members of the alliance could participate in the formulation of advice to the NATO council on nuclear policy. This committee received progress reports on the studies of the nuclear planning group of which Canada is a member. I would be prepared to table the communique of the meeting of the nuclear defence affairs committee if the house so desires.
I informed my colleagues in the N.D.A.C. that for Canada the main purpose of the changing strategic concept is to avoid excessive reliance on the early use of nuclear weapons for defence against aggression. We suggested that the political aspects of the problem be studied further.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The defence planning committee, which consists of ministers of all member countries except France, reviewed the work accomplished since their previous meeting in May, 1967. All ministers strongly endorsed the view, which was later reflected in the communique, that one of foundations for achieving an improvement in east-west relations and a peaceful settlement in Europe must be NATO's continuing defensive strength and capability to deter aggression.
Against this background the ministers considered the following main subjects: (a) the new strategic concept; (b) NATO force plans; (c) the standing naval force, Atlantic.
The new strategy of response against aggression makes provision for a flexible and balanced range of appropriate conventional and nuclear responses to all levels of aggression or threats of aggression. The ministers approved this concept.
External Affairs
For the first time the ministers adopted a five year rolling force plan. The current plan covers the period from 1968 to 1972. It includes a firm commitment of forces for 1968 and an outline of national plans for the period from 1969 to 1972.
As far as Canada is concerned, we reaffirmed the continued assignment for 1968 of our forces in Germany consisting of (a) the air division; (b) the Canadian mechanized brigade group. We also confirmed the continued availability from Canada for 1968 of
(a)	our already earmarked naval forces; (b) two brigades retained in Canada and already earmarked for Europe.
In respect of our plans after 1968 we proposed, as forecast in the white paper of 1964, to substitute one air transportable brigade group based in Canada for the two brigades now earmarked in Canada. We also outlined in general terms proposed reductions in the air division during the next few years. During the next year we shall be forming our new CF-5 squadrons for the support of mobile command forces. In doing this we plan to utilize the trained personnel which will become available as a result of later adjustments in the air division.
Hon. members will recall that when the original decision was made to earmark for SACEUR's strategic reserve two brigades stationed in Canada, it was envisaged that it would be feasible to transport this force to Europe in time to make a significant contribution. However, as a consequence of the gradual mechanization of our brigade in Germany and the corresponding changes in Canada, it has become increasingly apparent that the sea and air lift required to transport these forces to Europe in a mechanized form would not be available in time to be effective.
During the past few years the government examined a number of proposals to overcome this problem. One of these proposals involved the stockpiling in Europe of mechanized equipment for the balance of the force. Because of the expense and the impractical aspects, this proposal was dropped. As a result of the recent review of our military commitments both in Europe and elsewhere we have concluded that another proposal, that of an air transportable force, would be more appropriate and useful. As additional air transport becomes available this force, including men and equipment, can be transported to Europe in time to make an effective contribution. It would also provide us with

December 18. 1967
External Affairs
forces of sufficient flexibility to meet other requirements.
The new strategy of flexible response places more emphasis on dual-capable aircraft. Our air division has both a conventional and nuclear capability and thus is well suited to carry out the requirements of this new strategic concept.
The ministers also approved the organization of a new naval force. This force involves the transformation of the NATO Matchmaker naval training squadron into the standing naval force Atlantic consisting of six to eight destroyer type ships. Hon. members will recall that Matchmaker is a training squadron consisting of a number of ships from NATO countries in the Atlantic area. The squadron has been operating for the past few years and Canada has, from time to time, contributed a ship to it.
The major difference between Matchmaker and the standing naval force is that in Matchmaker ships joined the squadron for exercises; in the standing naval force they will be assigned for a given time and will be under the operational command of a NATO commander. Being composed of ships from various countries, the force will be a further visible evidence of NATO's solidarity.
Each participating country will assign a ship to the force for a fixed period during the year. Canada agrees with the concept of the force, and we are now studying the form of Canadian participation and expect to reach a decision shortly. Participation would not involve a new commitment but rather the assignment of one of the destroyers already earmarked for SACLANT to this NATO force.

I am
sure, Mr. Speaker, we all join in welcoming the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of National Defence back to Canada after their week in Brussels. I believe we have obtained more information about what went on there from the newspaper accounts than the ministers gave us in their reports today. However, I think everyone who takes an interest in this matter was delighted to note that the Harmel report was accepted by all the NATO countries, including France, so the unity of NATO was maintained at this time. I believe everyone was delighted, too, that the emphasis in the Harmel report was on further steps toward a detente in Europe.
[Mr. Cadieux (Terrebonne) .1
As the minister has said, and as we all agree, we hope these steps will go forward satisfactorily. The warning issued by the secretary general of NATO, Mr. Manlio Brosio in connection with the very large Soviet forces stationed in eastern Europe, the extension of their naval activities and particularly the increase in their naval strength in the Mediterranean, should be heeded because they pose a considerable threat so far as western Europe is concerned. These factors emphasize the necessity of maintaining military forces of NATO in a state of readiness so they will serve as a deterrent to any aggressive action, which is their main function.
The Minister of National Defence mentioned that a new strategy had been decided upon, but actually I feel this is not so much a new strategy as it is a reiteration or a more definite statement of a strategy which has been in effect for several years. I refer to the reliance on conventional forces, in the first instance at any rate, in the hope that their use will prevent the necessity of any nuclear attack being made or a nuclear response by either side. The five year force plan mentioned by the defence minister is to be in effect for the next five years, but he did not tell us what it is. I hope at some future time we will be able to get more details with regard to the five year force plan of NATO and particularly Canada's contribution to it.
The minister has said Canada's commitments for 1968 are unchanged, but there have been a considerable number of reports that the brigade in Europe is to be reduced by 500 men. Perhaps the minister could be more specific about that during the question period. I hope the proposed reduction in the air division has not been a unilateral decision on the part of Canada. There have been considerable rumours about a forthcoming reduction in the strength of the air division, and as I say whatever reductions are made in the coming years-there must be reductions because the aircraft are wearing out and crashing-I hope they will be made in consultation with our allies.
So far as the new destroyer force is concerned, as the minister rather indicated this seems to me to be more or less a realignment of forces already in existence. The minister did not say whether we were contributing one destroyer to this force, as has been rumoured, so I hope once more he will be in a position to give us some information.
December 18, 1967

[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to comment on this double barrelled announcement within the rules which require a brief statement; nevertheless I will try to stick to the rules. May I preface my remarks by welcoming both ministers back to the house. If they have been reading the newspapers they will have observed that however much the cold war in Europe is relaxing, the political wars in Canada seem to be heating up.
In his announcement the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to one feature of the discussions about NATO which are certainly welcome. That is to say, the minister said its attention is henceforth to be directed to what he called constructive areas of activity, arms control and disarmament measures. We hope this is just not words but that the statement will be followed by action, because for too long NATO has taken on the appearance of nothing but a military alliance. Unless the detente in Europe is exploited by NATO, I suggest that NATO is not going to have a very long life. Therefore I hope the announcement made by the minister in connection with these matters will be followed by a form of vigorous initiative.
In regard to the remarks by the Minister of National Defence, I should like to reiterate a suggestion that has been made from time to time in questions asked by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch); namely, that the two ministers appear as soon as possible before a joint meeting of the external affairs and national defence committees of this house so the matters they have raised can be examined in detail by hon. members.
In so far as the statement of the minister, as far as I understand it, represents a plan of the government gradually to opt out of the air division in Europe and to concentrate upon air transportability, the minister and hon. members know this is a course of action that we in this party have been recommending for years. We are glad to see there is action at last. As far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, our only regret is that the action is not more decisive and vigorous than this. We do not believe there continues to be any useful role for our nuclear armed brigade in Europe. We think the Canadian contribution should be in the form of a mobile conventional force based on Canada, and we believe this fits in with what the minister said is the new approach of NATO.
We trust, Mr. Speaker, that these new approaches will be given full and quick
External Affairs
implementation, because at this particular time in Canada's history I suggest we just cannot afford to be spending large sums of money on forms of defence that are either obsolete or no longer useful in meeting any existing threat in Europe.

Mr. Speaker, it is difficult in many respects to square the statements of the minister for external affairs with what we see. He is, as we all know, tremendously skilled at manoeuvring, but it will require more than all his adroitness to shore up NATO while at the same time attempting to make the treatment the organization has received from the French government in recent years seem a triumph rather than a disaster. We welcome the fact that the move to Brussels succeeded at all, but we should not pretend that this will have strengthened the organization or that it will function fully without the complete participation of France.
We also know, Mr. Speaker, that all this talk about disarmament is wishful thinking. The Soviet defence budget for 1968 is the greatest in its history of military expenditure. We realize that the economies of western Europe which have been lagging recently will not need any more encouragement in turning to defence production as a means of fueling those economies. This is still the best device in today's world to keep an economy going.
I suggest that one thing urgently needed, and which perhaps could be done through NATO, is a study of the effects of the economies of the world ceasing to embrace any military expenditure. The minister shows concern for military development, but I doubt that the ability of Canada to save Europe by airlifting our forces to that continent is anything more than a dream.
Rather than thinking of military development I suggest we might well think of the political moves we could make, even within NATO. Here I think of our rather ambiguous approach to Portugal and our shoring up of the Turkish-Greek dispute in Cyprus all these years while those two countries have diverted their NATO strength from its original purpose.

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: REPORT ON BLOOD INDIAN RESERVE
speechtext:
1. Dr. G. D.
Spindler prepared the material for chapters II and III entitled "Contemporary Blood Indian Community" and "Psychological Characteristics, Work Preferences and Values" respectively of the 22 chapter report on "The Economic Potential of the Blood Indian Reserve." (a) The full report contains an assessment of the resources of the Blood Indian Reserve, e.g. human, mineral, soils, rangeland, agriculture and suggests some methods by which these might be utilized to advantage.
(b)	Copies of the report were provided to the Blood band council who used it as a basis to undertake a more detailed study of matters relating to land use and economic development. December 18. 1967

My question, Mr. Speaker, is for the Minister of Finance. In the light of the statement by United States authorities and others who are members of the gold pool, and in the light of the recent statement by the governor of the Bank of Canada, would the minister now answer that portion of my question which he took as notice on Friday and advise Canada just where we stand on this question of the gold pool and international monetary relations?

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, December 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Trudeau for the second reading of Bill No. C-187, respecting divorce.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate was adjourned on Friday afternoon I was making the point that every responsible person believes that marriage should be a permanent relationship, seriously undertaken and with the full expectation of building a lifelong partnership. This is the ideal. I believe that most young couples have the idea that their union will be permanent, but the strains on marriage are very heavy today and many young couples are far from prepared to withstand those strains. Consequently, whether we like it or not there are very many marriages that fall by the wayside and many partnerships that prove not to be indissoluble.
Times have changed very greatly. When giving evidence to the committee on divorce Dr. Ollivier said that in the first 12 years after confederation parliament had enacted eight divorces, whereas in 1966 the Senate passed over 1,000 divorce resolutions. When we reflect on the fact that in 1966 people from only two provinces, Quebec and Newfoundland, were still coming to the Senate
December 18, 1967

with divorce petitions, we get some idea of the magnitude of the change. People from those two provinces alone brought to the Senate over 1,000 divorce petitions in 1966, and when we compare that with the eight divorces in all Canada which were enacted in the first 12 years after confederation we get some idea of the change.
I do not want to give the impression that there are not qualifications in this respect. In the first 12 years after confederation Canada was a very much smaller country and covered a great deal less territory than it does now. Also, the 1,000 divorce petitions in 1966 may have been many more than the number presented in a normal year from those two provinces. Nevertheless, times have changed greatly.
What is the situation today? We find that in Canada, whether we like it or not, no matter how much we may hope that all marriages will be permanent there are nearly half a million common law unions in which are not sanctioned in any way by marriage and the children of which are illegitimate. These unions have no position at all in law except in one or two very small respects. We also find there are very many couples, an undetermined number, who are held together in unhappy, strife-torn unions.

the hon. member would like me to talk of illegitimate parents I will be very happy to accommodate him. It is one of the easier places to accommodate him, I may say. There are very many couples who are held together in most unhappy unions or in unions from which all the respect and love that brought them together in the first place have gone. These couples are together simply because they cannot get free.
Of the many letters which I, along with other members of the house, have received I would like to read just two. They come from Vancouver, one from my constituency and one from the constituency of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Laing). However, they are symptomatic of the letters which come to us from all

across this country. One letter reads in part as follows:
May I tell you that for 14 years my wife and I have lived apart. There is no possibility of a reconciliation. There are no children or religious differences involved. Ours was a marriage which was unsuccessful from the outset notwithstanding we lived together on and off for 15 years.
My wife is gainfully employed and is approximately 58 years of age. I am also gainfully employed and am 59 years of age.
Over the years I have attempted to secure a divorce under the existing laws. My wife is not interested in divorce. She advised me on many occasions that I could live with who I liked, but she would not agree under any circumstances to a divorce.
I believe I am a law-abiding citizen and of temperate and/or moderate habits. Surely the divorce laws will be amended to permit a person in my situation, and I believe there are thousands of us, to secure a proper divorce in order to attempt to live a normal life, and take a proper place in society.
May I urge you to be compassionate and understanding of the many people who, through no desire of their own, entered into marriages that did not work out successfully, and yet under existing laws are powerless to have such unhappy unions dissolved.
We have an example here of a union which was simply unsuccessful, where the partners failed to develop those human relationships that would have made the marriage successful, where there appears to be very little recrimination or bitterness but there is a settled conviction on the part of the husband that there cannot be a reconciliation. The wife evidently cares very little about the marriage because she has told him he can live with whom he likes but that she will not enable him to obtain a divorce.
In my opinion this is a very good example of the many hundreds of letters which all of us have received from people who want to be free. Frankly, I consider it is immoral to compel two such people to go on living together in a relationship which certainly does not make for happiness.

I want to come to that in a moment because I realize this is just one example of many hundreds of people who have been waiting and waiting in a very law-abiding and patient way for the new divorce legislation which will give them release. In this case it will give the husband release and will provide release also for his wife, even though

apparently she does not want that release. I think much of her reluctance may stem from the fact she feels that under existing conditions it will not be recognized by the community as being a proper thing to do. The other letter is quite different. It is from a woman in my constituency who says in part:
I am one of thousands of deserted women in this country who have no hope of obtaining my freedom while the present laws exist. No one has seen or heard of my husband since he left us three and a half years ago. Only his creditors really looked very hard, but they gave up. I cannot prove adultery although it was well known he left with a woman who took half her husband's bank account with her. However!
My children are now six years and four and a half years old and lovely children. I do not attempt to meet anyone else because to me there is no point. That would probably end up in a common law relationship. This I do not desire for myself or children. But I can see why so many people are forced into this type of situation. With the problems a woman alone has to face in society, it can happen just from sheer human need.

I believe that this woman also can be helped by the new legislation, and I point out that here is a very fine type of woman indeed. Even if she could do so she does not want to expose herself to the temptations of a common law relationship because she does not want her children to grow up in such an atmosphere.
Fears have been expressed that the new legislation might tempt people to rush into divorce unduly and thus destroy the sanctity of marriage. But here we have a woman who has been waiting patiently for some years and who values the sanctity of marriage to the point that she does not wish to enter into a relationship which would violate her conception of a proper marriage because she does not wish her children to grow up under those circumstances.
I am sure that these two people and many others like them will be feeling gratitude now that the new legislation is on the point of being passed. I think we should express our appreciation to the minister in this regard. These marriages are dead and there is no hope of reviving them.
What must we do for people who find themselves in this situation at the present time? Two things can be done. We can either refuse to widen the grounds for divorce, pretend that a need for it does not exist and persist in festooning dead marriages with funeral flowers. In other words, we would go on perpetuating an immoral situation. Marriages that have failed have been called an

unholy deadlock. I call them unholy wedlock. The other alternative is to do what the government is now preparing to do, to update our divorce legislation and in a measure at least clean up the hypocrisy which has surrounded the problem of broken marriages for so long.
Although I was not a member of the committee on divorce and consequently was not present at their deliberations, nervertheless I have learned that two concepts are embodied in the bill before us. One of them is the concept of matrimonial offences which I call the theory of crime and punishment. It consists of a number of offences, any one or a combination of which would enable people to apply for a divorce with a reasonable hope of getting it. Until now adultery has been the only ground for divorce in Canada, whereas now other grounds have been added, one of which is marriage breakdown. This is a completely new concept. Under this concept, when a marriage is dead and can be proved to be dead for a number of reasons and when the court upon suitable advice and investigation finds that a marriage is dead, a divorce may be granted on the ground of marriage breakdown. The two concepts, marriage breakdown and matrimonial offence are contained in the same piece of legislation.
Like the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and other hon. members who have spoken, I would have preferred to see us do away with this patchwork quilt of various matrimonial offences and to judge marriage on the sole ground of breakdown based on the various factors which have contributed to the breakdown. I believe a marriage should be judged on the basis of whether or not a human relationship has failed beyond the possibility of reconciliation. I believe that henceforth marriage breakdown should be the sole ground for divorce in Canada. We should avoid having to go through the 30 years of experience which Britain had to go through after having combined the concepts of matrimonial offences and marriage breakdown in one piece of legislation. I believe that Britain's experience has proven to the satisfaction of the British people that it does not work. This is demonstrated by the fact at the present time that country is on the verge of introducing in parliament a new bill whereby divorce may be granted solely on grounds of marriage breakdown. We found, for the first time in my experience, that the people who did not want to use this new legislation themselves were nevertheless willing that other Canadians who would make use of such information should have it.
We hope, Mr. Speaker, that within a few days we shall see the minister introduce legislation which will change the law relating to birth control in such a way as to leave it open to the individual conscience as to the use to be made of birth control knowledge or legislation. At the same time no one would be forced to accept this knowledge or these devices if their conscience did not permit them to do so. I believe this would be a good solution for Canada. Incidentally, I would be remiss in my duty if I did not express my appreciation of the stand of the churches in these fields of social legislation. The churches have given leadership in these fields. The churches have recognized that times have changed. They have realized that if they are going to help people they must do so in a very practical way.
In connection with birth control it was most interesting that the Canadian conference of Catholic bishops came before our committee when we were discussing birth control legislation. They said that they themselves were not too interested in changing the law on birth control but they knew the present law was unenforceable and that when a law is unenforceable it is bad legislation because it brings about disrespect for the law. They gave us the green light to go ahead and make the changes for the people who want the changes and whose conscience will permit them to use the information.
It would be my hope that before we have finished the discussions on abortion now taking place we would find that every church would be prepared to go that far. A number of them have already done so. I should like to see the other churches which have not yet committed themselves or have not yet appeared before our committee make it possible for those people who so desire to have the abortion laws liberalized.
I should like to say a word now about divorce. I was pleased when I read the report of the joint committee on divorce to find these words:
Witnesses before your committee have stressed:
"That those whose religious principles are against

divorce in any form should no longer be able to impose restrictions on the personal lives of those whose principles differ in this respect".
This view has been unchallenged and the representatives of the churches appearing before your committee have wholeheartedly endorsed it. "The Christian church no longer has the right to force its views on a pluralistic society", declared the Baptist Federation of Canada, a view endorsed by the Catholic Women's League of Canada.
I want to quote from their brief:
While we do not believe in divorce ourselves we cannot expect the laws of this country to be used in such a manner as to prevent those who, unlike ourselves, do not believe that marriage is monogamous and indissoluble, from acting in accordance with their own religious convictions... We would also emphasize that while we have beliefs in the matter of marriage, we do not wish to impose those beliefs on the entire Canadian society through the medium of civil law.
On this permissive basis of allowing people to use this legislation when their conscience permits and not forcing it on people whose consciences do not permit, we are prepared to accept this new divorce legislation. I should like, of course, to see it go farther. Unfortunately the minister has put it at the point where he thinks he has a Canadian consensus. As the law goes into practice I would like to see the emphasis shifted more and more from the crime and punishment matrimonial offences basis to the marriage breakdown basis. I am convinced we shall get there before too long in this country. I believe the main points we must safeguard now have to do with the children of the marriage partners. Almost equally important are measures which must be taken, probably within the provinces, to see that the cost of divorce is brought down within the means of those people who would like to use this legislation.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Before I conclude I should like to congratulate the minister on being able to get this legislation before the house at long last. I should not like to leave congratulations without referring to some of the men who helped keep alive for so many years the idea that we needed this legislation. I believe that the co-chairman of the divorce committee, Senator Roebuck, will feel that his long life has indeed been crowned by the achievement of this type of legislation. Reference was made to Senator Aseltine who got a bill through the other place which sought to widen the grounds for divorce but unfortunately died on the order paper of this chamber. I should also like to refer to the hon. members for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and Timiskaming (Mr. December 18, 1987

Peters) who, unpopular though their efforts may have been at the time, nevertheless kept alive the need for this legislation to be brought into being so as to get divorce out of parliament and into the place where it belongs, the courts of this country.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to the person who perhaps more than anybody else started the agitation for modern divorce laws in this country. I refer to my father, the late J. S. Woodsworth, who in 1928 when there were nearly 300 divorce petitions, 95 per cent of them from Ontario, clogging up the machinery both of this house and the other place, turned himself into a single Horatius at the bridge, if you will, and as every divorce bill came up for discussion talked about it, examined it, asked about the children and made a complete and utter nuisance of himself in the interests of getting those divorce petitions out of the house and into a place where they could receive proper consideration. His final tribute was the passage of his own bill in 1928 to provide for divorce courts in Ontario.
All these and many others, Mr. Speaker, have helped over the years to achieve this legislation, and it needed the efforts of every one of them and many whom I have not mentioned. This bill is a real step forward. I hope we shall go the rest of the way before too many years have gone by and that we shall discover that this divorce legislation is not going to destroy or weaken marriage in this country. Marriage is far too important an institution for that.
I also hope this legislation will do what a number of us believe it will do, aid in building and strengthening personal responsibility on the part of individual men and women. For personal responsibility on the part of ordinary men and women, Mr. Speaker, there is no substitute.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house now has before it a bill to reform the Divorce Act in which many people are concerned. I hardly need to add that the most concerned are precisely those involved in this dilemma, who are waiting for the house to carry out amendments and pass new legislation which will not so much facilitate obtaining a divorce but make clearer and more realistic the grounds for divorce.
Like many members, I have received briefs and opinions. I have picked among the best elements brought to my attention and I shall use the very same words and phrases, so as to avoid changing their value or meaning.
I received in my office people involved in matrimonial problems who feel that only a divorce would enable them to reorganize their lives, but the requirements of the act were in no way in accordance with their means.
Being of the Roman Catholic faith and brought up in the observance of religious principles that were taught us, it would have been difficult for me, even a few years ago, to take position on such an issue, because it was said that only the death of one of the spouses could dissolve the bond of matrimony. Today, it should not be imagined that canon law has been changed or that the oecumenic council has changed the religion, not at all. The council has mitigated the legislation, eased the standards, but has never changed anything else. On this point I take the liberty of quoting an article published in the Medicine Hat News and reprinted in La Presse on April 24 1967, and I quote:
Increased tolerance.
The Catholic bishops of Canada are to be congratulated on having withdrawn their opposition to the mitigation of civil divorce legislation in the country.
The brief of the Canadian Catholic Conference on this occasion emphasizes that for the Church, the bonds of matrimony are sacred and that civil authority has no power to dissolve them. They add that Canada is a multidenominational country and that the present civil law is open to abuse.
This is surely a welcome proof of increased religious tolerance in Canada. And that is the hub of the problem. No one can deny the Catholic

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
Church the right to have its own laws on matrimony. It is only when the Church attempts to block a bill involving both non-members and members of the Catholic Church that a conflict arises-
The bishops' brief removes one of the last obstacles to government intervention. When the sittings of the divorce committee will come to an end, the federal government will no longer have any excuse to abstain from legislating.
I feel bound today, as a legislator, to try to make my humble contribution to this debate and may God guard me from any blunder which might bring on me the anathema of the legislators of my church. Besides, the religious authorities of various provinces will be able to accept and endorse or reject the new civil law. In the meantime, it can be said that the basis of the present Divorce Act is not sound. It considers divorce as a relief granted to the innocent party, because of an offence committed by the guilty party.
Experience teaches us that only adultery which, in most provinces, is considered as an offence against the nature of marriage, constitutes grounds for divorce, and yet, adultery is only one form of offence, among others, which can cause the failure of marriage. There are many other forms of offences and their seriousness can vary considerably. Marriages have been broken up through offences other than adultery, and the present legislation tends to increase the bitterness and antagonism, because in divorce proceedings, how often is there agreement between the parties concerned. An adultery is invented and staged in connivance with the parties involved and the witnesses are paid to give evidence before the courts of what they saw and heard. To begin with, we must ensure a stricter enforcement of this condition which seems to the advantage of better-off, and give those of slender means opportunity to submit their grievances to the same courts.
I support the concept under which divorce is the legal and true recognition of the breakdown of marriage. Valid methods will then have to be developed to ascertain the failure, and a proper period of separation provided to show that the situation is lasting.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
It might be necessary to consider other matrimonial offences-because they are at a negative level-such as sexual intercourse including manifestations of sadism, acts of cruelty on the person of the spouse or the children, or de facto desertion. As far as desertion is concerned, it will be necessary to consider the whole of Canada as the domicile and not the evidence of domicile from one
[Mr. Thomas (Maisonneuve-Rosemont).!
province to the other. Besides the bill stipulates as much.
Mr. Speaker, even if I recognize that various matrimonial offences are committed, I find it difficult to admit that their simple existence constitutes grounds for the dissolution of a marriage, as the system of proceedings permits it. First of all, each major category of offences considered includes various situations which are greatly different. There is a fundamental difference between adultery committed on an impulse, as an isolated act, and a series of continuous adventures, or yet a liaison used to hurt and aggravate the spouse.
Similarly, there is a tremendous difference between blows given under provocation and maintaining a permanent attitude of anger and hostility, an attitude that can lead periodically to blows or that tortures the other spouse or the children and which manifests itself through verbal maliciousness as cruel as blows.
Experience has taught us this:	when
spouses discuss the causes leading their marriage to a dead-end, doubtless they throw violent accusations at each other but almost invariably they come to recognize, in some way or other, their respective share of the blame for reaching that situation. When they discuss divorce, it seems that the requirements of the law make them feel ill at ease, which leads them into presenting a cooked up version of the facts.
I think too that mental illness should be considered in the same way as physical illness and, to my mind, it is contrary to common sense and conscience to consider an illness as an offence or as grounds for divorce in itself. The presence of the spouse or children as well as the nature of the relationship between them may be one of the factors largely contributing to the recovery of the sick person. On the other hand, strained matrimonial relations may have contributed to the development of the illness.
The same applies in the case of a criminal. When a spouse must serve a sentence, even a long one, this does not involve a matrimonial offence but it involves going from a legislation and a procedure based on the matrimonial offence concept to a legislation and procedure based on the concept of matrimonial breakdown.
The hub of the problem consists in developing adequate means to prove such marriage breakdown. Proper application of the
December 18, 1967

legislation will depend mainly on the adequacy of the tests to establish the fact.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I am asking divine providence to enlighten our leaders so as to pass just and equitable legislation for all, because all must be equal before the law.

[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I happen to be one of those who are convinced that there is a good deal to be said for the marriage breakdown concept. Some call it the marriage breakdown theory, but it is not a theory. In my opinion this parliament or other parliaments will some day accept that concept. I have sympathy for the minister inasmuch as he has not had the benefit of experience in this area that others in other jurisdictions have had and therefore has not seen fit to make the drastic change of incorporating the marriage breakdown concept in the bill as the sole ground for divorce. But I do want to say at this point that just because one or two members of the party of which I am glad to be a member happen to be interested in the marriage breakdown concept does not in any way say we do not view this major reform in our social legislation with a very great deal of enthusiasm and are not anxious to join in supporting the bill as its various stages are passed by parliament. I think that is pretty clear to those who sit over here. Just because we have individual views on the method of reform does not in any way detract from our very great approval for Bill C-187.
As a one-time practising lawyer I wish to say I feel that most of my brethren will find the role of conciliator, as envisioned in clause 7, really not a very good answer to the many requests of church groups and others interested in divorce reform for a meaningful attempt at marriage counselling and marriage conciliation. One hon. member has spoken about the system in Australia. I hoped something like that would be made part of this bill, but I share the view of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) that many lawyers, not because of any wish to circumvent the law but because of the pressure of business and the fact that they are not trained as marriage counsellors, will make the provisions of clause 7 a rather routine proceeding. This, I think, would be a pity.
However, speaking for myself I wish to say I found that when husbands and wives, or one or other of them, approached me seeking my services the marriage had long since passed the point that efforts to reconcile the differences would have been of any assistance. Although I recognize that in most instances this would be a provincial responsibility I has hoped that through a joint federal-provincial effort a more meaningful type of marriage counselling service could have been provided.

I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and other hon. members to forgive me if I make one point having to do with the jurisdiction in my own province. I asked the minister a question about this point at an earlier stage during the course of his speech. Clause 2 (e) gives a definition of court, and in New Brunswick it is given as "the trial division or branch of the supreme court of the province." In my own province a single judge sits as a judge of divorce and matrimonial causes in only one city, the capital of New Brunswick, and I have heard rumblings to the effect that despite the definition provided in this bill the responsible officials in that province will attempt to circumvent what I am sure is the clear intention of parliament by maintaining the present system.
Speaking for many people in the legal profession in New Brunswick and also speaking as a representative of the people in at least one of its constituencies, 1 must say I would hope very sincerely that upon the enactment of this legislation all judges of the Queen's Bench division of the province of New Brunswick, as they make their circuits, will be hearing divorce matters. It would be a very great pity if this were not the case.
I think that over the next two or three years we have to be prepared for a large increase of petitions for divorce because this legislation will seek to remedy the very serious problems that have been enunciated not only by hon. members in this debate but also by very many people and institutions who presented briefs to the parliamentary committee on divorce. But I do not think we should be alarmed. I am sure those of us who have made some study of the subject will not be alarmed by a large increase. I hope others will not be put off should this happen. I hope we will all recognize that in many instances an opportunity for relief is being given to very many people who are suffering severe hardships and handicaps as to their own status and the status of their children simply because for 100 years the law of divorce in Canada has been so pernicious. I share the views of those who anxiously look forward to the clarification of the status of so many children through the instrument of a reformed divorce law.
I know that a vast majority of members of parliament will support the bill. I know they will do so conscious of the sanctity of marriage, conscious of the need to strengthen the family as the basic unit of our society, but conscious too that there has been a very evident need for reform and that we but do

our duty by responding to the initiative, taken by the divorce committee and the minister, to try to bring some relief where it has been so obviously needed for so long.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the new divorce legislation has been well accepted everywhere, and rightly so, because it brings fundamental changes that have been awaited and desired for a long time by a large part of public opinion. It replaces provisions that have become old fashioned and obsolete, particularly in our present social climate.
I had the pleasure and the benefit of sitting on the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to consider the whole question of divorce and of sitting on its steering committee. Whe have received a lot of very interesting briefs, particularly from various religious denominations. Under the chairmanship of Senator Roebuck, well versed in the question and gifted with a rare energy and lucidity of mind for a man of his years, and assisted by one of our most distinguished colleagues, the hon. member for High Park (Mr. Cameron), this committee sat most actively and, on June 20 last, presented a report which has certainly helped and guided the Minister of Justice (Mr. Trudeau), as he himself indicated.
As a member of a religious denomination advocating indissolubility of marriage, I was greatly interested and impressed by the logical and realistic attitude taken by the Canadian Catholic Episcopate in its brief presented before the committee. A distinction is made especially between the moral or religious order and the civil or political order. While upholding the permanence of the conjugal bond, they recognize that civil authorities, under certain conditions, have the right to make the present legislation, more flexible as requested by a great number of citizens, for the common good of the civil society.
That new attitude of the church was surely inspired by the principles of religious freedom adopted at the second Vatican council, in December 1965, when the resolution proclaiming that man is entitled to religious freedom was passed.
Since, at the religious level, our country is a clearly pluralistic community, a pluralistic society, that freedom must be guarded more closely than ever and to confuse civil and religious legislation could easily be a source of misunderstanding and uneasiness.
December 18. 1967



Besides, as pointed out by the Minister of Justice, this is an act which will allow the dissolution of the civil tie of marriage but, of course, it does force anyone to remarry if that goes against moral or religious convictions.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
If, as has been suggested, civil authorities are fully entitled to legislate in divorce matters, it must be kept in mind, however, that the family is the fundamental unit of society and that it is essential to do everything possible to preserve and maintain it. Divorce should only be a measure of last resort, taken after every possible means has been used to avoid a Anal breakdown.
Several other religious groups have expressed the same views, as concerns education and preparation for marriage, and promoting appropriate organizations designed to reconcile spouses experiencing difficulties. Those proposals are sound and worthwhile, of course, but are not easy to implement, because of the conAict of jurisdiction in such matters, and they concern rather the civil rights of the parties involved; this is rather a provincial matter and it might be advisable for the governments to deal with this important aspect of family relations when they meet for consultations or conferences on the constitution and its amendments.
However, the bill under study has provided, in many instances, for procedures of conciliation and it grants extended powers to the courts with a view to encouraging reconciliation between the spouses who will be granted a divorce only when it is certain that a reconciliation is impossible.
I have reservations about the efficiency of some of those means, but time and practice only will allow us to judge, and the law can then be improved accordingly. The report of the joint committee and the present legislation both recognized the wish of the state to maintain marriage as the basic institution of society and as its source of stability, but for those who believe in the dissolution of a union that has become unbearable or unendurable, the grounds for divorce have been duly extended in order to eliminate mainly the well-known effects of the present situation and also offer an opportunity to legalize the situation for thousands of Canadians living now under common law marriage.
I believe also that the government was right in following the recommendations of the joint committee and in rejecting the principle of marriage breakdown as grounds for
Divorce Law Reform
divorce, as recommended by some reports submitted to the committee and by a few committee members. This theory may seem attractive at Arst sight, but I think that our courts would have too much freedom, too much leeway, and we would incur the risk of having excessive or inadequate interpretations depending, of course, on the area of the country concerned, and that would surely lead to confusion, uncertainty and inconsistent court Andings.
It was more prudent and more realistic, for the time being at least, to provide the courts with some guidelines, some speciAc orientation for granting divorce when evidence of matrimonial offences or marriage breakdown is produced, pursuant to the provisions of the legislation. As it is, our courts are not yet organized, and they lack the expert or investigative services required for the application of such a formula.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not dwell upon the grounds for divorce listed in clauses 3 and 4 of the bill. They reproduce in the main the worthwhile and logical recommendations made by the joint committee. Practice and experience will show us whether these provisions should be revised later, always, of course, subject to the rigorous and explicit condition stipulated in the law, which is that divorce will only be granted if the court decides that	there	is no hope	of
reconciliation.
Mr. Speaker, I have more serious reservations or doubts concerning corollary relief measures, in the present circumstances, particularly with regard to the division of property, alimony and the custody and care of children. With a few other members of the committee, we tried in vain to introduce amendments to alter the recommendations of the committee in this connection. However, I note with pleasure that, in the present legislation, no reference has been made to the separate maintenance of spouses and since it is a matter concerning property, it will continue to come under the provincial laws.
For the moment, and as long as the provincial authorities do not decide to establish courts to deal with family problems, as I suggested, I wonder whether, in the case of the province of Quebec especially, it would not have been advisable, to avoid any confusion and any conAict of jurisdiction, to restrict ourselves to the problem of divorce as such and follow the practice existing for years and under which parliament has never looked after matters of alimony and custody

December 18. 1987
Divorce Law Reform
of children which have been settled by the competent courts, most of the time by the superior court in the district where the spouses are living following an action for separation in accordance with the Civil Code. This will certainly create some ambiguous and unfortunate situations, for example, if a decision has already been made in connection with the alimony or the custody of children before the superior court and if, thereafter, an action for divorce has been lodged before the exchequer court and a party has obtained contradictory orders. Even if the orders delivered in accordance with clauses 10 and 11 of the legislation can be registered before the superior court and carried out as orders of that court, in my opinion, some practical difficulties and perhaps some detrimental delays could occur, if changes are required under the orders as a result, for example, of a change in the state or condition of the parties.
I think that this whole problem should be considered and I presume that the Minister of Justice will consult with the provincial authorities, especially on matters of procedure or rules on practices to follow.
At this time, I will merely raise another important point in the bill, that is the change in jurisdiction. Until now, citizens of Quebec and Newfoundland who wanted a divorce had to present their petition to parliament and, since 1963, to the Senate especially where, after hearing the petitions, a commissioner made reports to the Senate.
Now, these petitions will be presented to a division of the exchequer court, until the province of Quebec decides to present them to the superior court, as provided by clause 22 of the bill, where other suggestions are also made.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
It is a happy amendment which should above all reduce considerably the cost of getting a divorce. That will abolish the discrimination which existed against people without much money.
That division of the exchequer court will sit at any time and anywhere in Canada. That should facilitate hearings, but since this will be, I suppose, travelling court and will be without the necessary services or machinery to discharge duties or execute its orders, I hope that this will be a temporary provision and that, following consultations with the province of Quebec or within the framework of the amendments to the constitution, if it is not possible to transfer the whole field of marriage and divorce to the provinces to

maintain a perfect uniformity in the country or for other reasons, at least our provincial authorities will very shortly create real courts which will have jurisdiction over all problems concerning the family, including divorce.
These courts would be presided by judges who would have taken specialized courses in domestic relations and who would be assisted by experts such as psychiatrists, social workers, doctors, etc. Thus they could consider family problems as a whole, whereas at present these problems may have to be handled by several courts or jurisdictions, either civil or criminal, depending on whether separation, custody of children, refusal to provide alimony, etc. are involved.
This, Mr. Speaker, would be in the best interests of the family. Moreover, it would take place in an atmosphere conducive to the best possible settlement of family problems both legally and socially.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that there will be in the future, some agreement between the provincial authorities and the federal government in respect of jurisdiction, in order to prevent this mix-up and this confusion which make it impossible to take any concerted and planned action in this important field of human relations. Since divorce and its related problems will always be with us and be of concern to a greater number of our citizens, why not recognize this undeniable fact and, at last, make available to those who are entitled to this privilege and who wish to use it, the most complete and the best organized means to achieve this end, which, after all, Mr. Speaker, would only strengthen the very institution of marriage?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house and the country were presented with a variety of views on divorce at the committee hearings and I had hoped that as a result of the recommendations of that committee and the deliberations put forward the government would have had the sense to present what I would consider a better bill. As a lawyer I am appalled by some of the provisions of this bill and I will make some reference to them. I have my own views with regard to the sanctity of marriage, the preservation of family life and the purpose of this legislation, and naturally they may not coincide with the ideas of every member in the house.
December 18. 1967

I was very gravely disappointed that the government saw fit to apply the pressures of government sanction without allowing a free vote on a matter of this kind. To me the question of divorce is as important as abortion, and is as important or more important than capital punishment. Yet members are being blackjacked in this regard by party positions having to be taken. I can only say I regret that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) did not, having said that members would be free to express themselves and to vote as they wished, avail himself of the opportunity to allow them to do so. This whole matter has now been made subject to limited party positions. We know very well that the whip will be used. This is a very queer way for the minister to suggest that moral views should not apply. I wonder what sort of moral eunuchs he thinks we are, that we can be bland and take other than an objective position in respect of a matter so fundamental as marriage and the dissolution of marriage.
I recognize that everyone has a right to his own opinion, and from the beginning I have felt there are many areas in which our marriage and divorce laws should be changed. I am not suggesting I am a devotee of what I think has unfortunately taken hold of some of our colleagues in this house in respect of galloping, permissive morality. Their attitude is that as long as people want to do something let them go ahead, as long as they feel they should not be married let them put their marriages asunder. I have in mind particularly some of the extensive remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) I simply cannot agree with the type of morality that allows people to go ahead and get a divorce whenever they want. I think we must have a certain sense of responsibility and that there are norms to which society must conform. I would not like it to be said that we are instituting in this country a form of marriage and divorce legislation which would ultimately lead to consecutive polygamy, in other words, to something akin to the coupling of rabbits or the mating of mink.
I have seen a number of judges performing, if I may use that term advisedly, and I know their view is such that they will not decide whether a man and woman shall remain together. I know the view they will take in respect of this measure; this measure can become merely a convenient vehicle for consecutive polygamy or divorce by consent. If we go all the way with the concept of the
Divorce Law Reform
breakdown of marriage being the main or sole ground for divorce-and this bill makes a mockery of reconciliation proceedings- then the decision will be taken by the parties themselves, because that will be the evidence put before the court. This evidence will reflect the attitude and the views of the parties, not the results of extensive investigation by the courts. There is no machinery whatsoever to provide for such investigation.
In case anyone should suggest that clause 7 imposes any degree of reconciliation machinery, let me say that this is patently wrong. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) referred to what he called the farce of the "three C's" and said that the answers to the questions involved were stereotyped. I can readily visualize the affidavits of counsel pursuant to clause 7. They will indicate that the lawyer has brought to the attention of the parties those provisions regarding conciliation and that the clients have been informed of marriage counselling and guidance facilities known to the lawyer.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Let me tell the minister that as a junior counsel I did a good deal of this type of work. In addition I was a member of the board of the Edmonton family service bureau and in every case with which I was associated I asked my clients whether they had gone to that family service bureau. I said, "I will make the appointment for you." In most cases they did consult social workers or family service workers. For some that was the end of it. But many more came back because, they said, the other party would not go. All I would have to do to comply with this clause would be to put in an affidavit that I had informed the client that there was available this or that bureau and had discussed with him the possibility of a reconciliation with his spouse. All I would have to do would be to ask the client, "Would you consider reconciliation with your spouse?" That is all I would have to do; that would constitute a discussion.
Clause 8 deals with the court's inquiry. I have pointed out to the minister that in my humble estimation this procedure will be totally inadequate for true, meaningful reconciliation. Knowing the attitude of certain men on the bench who say it is not their purpose to keep a man and woman together, I say that this provision will become perfunctory and therefore meaningless in our law.
554$

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
I am not saying there are no conscientious men on the bench but I know there are many who are not that conscientious with regard to these matters. Divorce has never been a palatable subject for most judges. As a matter of fact, I know a good many eminent counsel who would have been excellent judges but who told me that under no circumstances would they consider accepting an appointment to the bench because they would have to sit on divorce cases. They had no moral scruples with regard to divorce but took this position because of a personal distaste. The same thing applies with regard to lawyers who have said they would never accept an appointment to the bench, if one was offered to them, because they would have to sit on capital cases and did not want to sit in judgment on a man's life. This was their personal approach.
I want to come back to the gounds for divorce that are opened up in this bill. I point out immediately to the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway that the grounds for divorce as they exist today in this country are not limited to adultery. As a matter of fact, the grounds that appear in paragraphs (a) and (b) of clause 3 are applicable in most provinces where divorce is allowed. I have had experience of this in the province of Alberta. This bill has introduced the strange anomaly of a marriage offence, not as an additional ground but merely as a ground for divorce that a person has gone through a form of marriage with another, without anything further. There does not have to be any sexual relationship.
Subclauses (a) and (b) of clause 3 talk about sexual offences or sexual aberrations, and then we have the mere going through of a form of marriage without anything further, whether or not it was culpable as would be the case in order to found a charge of bigamy under the Criminal Code. We know people have been innocently involved in a second form of marriage because they thought they had the right to marry and there was not sufficient evidence to establish a charge of bigamy. In such cases there may have been nothing more than a form of marriage and yet a provision is introduced in the bill establishing this as a marital offence; one might say one of the mortal sins of married life. I say this because clause 3 really consists of, shall we say, the major offences, and in clause 4 are the additional grounds, somewhat less than those contained in clause 3 but still sufficient to establish grounds for divorce.

Then we come to the question of physical and mental cruelty. With this provision I agree, with the reservation that I trust we shall not have that burned toast concept of mental cruelty which seems sufficient for some courts to grant a divorce, or that rather odd, eccentric conduct that shall be deemed to be mental cruelty a la Hollywood or of the type on which some jurisdictions are prepared to grant divorces. I am surprised the government did not follow the example of the British act and include incurable insanity as a ground for divorce. Perhaps it can be argued that clause 9 (3) establishes insanity because it deals with separation and its continuance. This is a sort of back door approach, if I am right in what is intended to be included in the bill.
Two psychiatrists spoke to me last week and said they hoped they would be able to write to me and make representations that incurable insanity be deemed to be a ground for divorce. According to their reading of the bill this was not provided in it. The minister may be able to point out to me where I have missed it in the bill, but with the greatest respect I have not been able to find it. We then come to the additional grounds contained in clause 9 (3).

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: Insanity for how long?

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I said incurable insanity. The word "incurable" has only one meaning. If it is intended that there shall be hope of rehabilitation, I am greatly surprised at the interpretation of "hope " contained in clause 4 (1) (b) where the following words are used:
-and there is no reasonable expectation of the respondent's rehabilitation within a reasonably foreseeable period;
We must remember that in these circumstances a divorce will probably be granted In other words, the expectation of the respondent's rehabilitation is hopeless within a reasonably foreseeable period. But when we were dealing with the death penalty and the abolition thereof the Prime Minister said there is no man who can be deemed to be hopeless for rehabilitation. These words have been used with regard to the death penalty but with respect to divorce, if a man is an alcoholic or a drug addict it does not take much to declare him hopeless, I am wondering why we must apply different standards to "hope".
December 18, 1967

[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Also, I find it rather incongruous to see introduced in a bill on divorce a ground for nullity which until now has presented no difficulties whatsoever. If a marriage has not been consummated it is not a marriage but merely a form of it. The jurisprudence has been in existence for generations that nonconsummation is a ground for nullity. Then why introduce it into a divorce bill?
There is another aspect of the bill which I must confess I find strange and on which I would have liked to hear the opinion of the Canadian Bar Association and of some other legal authorities. I refer to domicile. Nowhere in the bill is domicile defined except by inference under clause 6 in which we are asked to accept the definition of domicile of any jurisdiction in the world, including Las Vegas, Reno and Tijuana, Mexico. Under clause 6 we are to recognize foreign decrees based on domicile as locally defined and Canadians have the right to remarry as long as the law of the jurisdiction in which the decree for divorce was granted states that the parties were domiciled there.
For example, under the law in Nevada a divorce may be granted after six week's residence there, which is equivalent to domicile. In Tijuana, Mexico, I believe it is possible to file papers for a divorce on the basis of attorning to that jurisdiction. Is that what we are prepared to accept in Canada? This provision will introduce all sorts of complications. I may be wrong and I am subject to persuasion otherwise but I would say that this bill introduces more problems than it tends to cure from a legal point of view, although not necessarily a social point of view. When it comes to the application of the law it is difficult to distinguish between legal and social effects. It will be remembered that if the bill goes through unmodified, all Canadians will be subject to what I consider to be a legal horror because of the difficulties it will introduce.
There is one provision in the bill on which I wish to commend the minister, namely, the provision for the extension of jurisdiction for divorce to courts in provinces which at the present time do not have that jurisdiction. I think this is a logical and reasonable extension. However, that is the best I can say for the bill.
On the whole I would have liked to see a much better bill brought forward, with less rush imposed on us. It is true that there were many committee hearings at which numerous
Divorce Law Reform,
witnesses and various organizations were allowed to bring forward their recommendations with regard to marriage and divorce. I would have liked more people to speak about making it more difficult to get married and about preparation for marriage. Under this legislation it will be as easy to discard a spouse as to take one, which we know is relatively easy. One could do it as easily as buying a suit and discarding it after a period of wear. I do not think, with all due respect, that this is what we should be legislating for.
I grant you, sir, that there are many situations in which appropriate amendments to our law could have been made, but I say to the government that it should have taken the precaution of putting forward its proposals for examination by judicial bodies and others who could have commented on them. This legislation will have a long lasting effect. To have a proposal imposed upon the house and to ask the house to act on it under the pressure of a pending Christmas adjournment is totally wrong. I am not at all concerned about the government's desire for speed in passing this legislation. This is a very important piece of legislation because it affects all the people in this country much more than does, for example, the Broadcasting Act or the taxation bills, and yet we are asked to rush it along. I find this to be a rather strange attitude on the part of the government.
