subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first word is to thank the hon. members from all parties for their constructive attitude in this discussion.
From all sides valuable comments have been made on this legislation and I have felt a sincere desire by all to improve it and to achieve a truly modern and useful divorce act for our country.
At this stage I could not reply in detail to all the questions that have been brought up. I believe I shall have the opportunity to do so during consideration in committee, but I should now like to touch upon three general questions which are also the questions that cropped up most often during the comments by the various members.

December 18, 196?
Divorce Law Reform
The first question bears on the issues of the breakdown of marriage and reconciliation procedure. The second bears on jurisdiction of the courts, for instance, the suggestion that was brought forward several times to give jurisdiction to county courts. The third question deals with conflicting legislation, for instance, between this legislation and the Civil Code of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say generally that all those questions can be answered by a single comment, namely that such matters give rise to very difficult problems with regard to federal-provincial relations.
Those are questions that cannot be answered without taking into account the conflicts of jurisdiction and that cannot be solved if the complexity of the federal system is overlooked. It is really a field where cooperative federalism is called for, and it is in that spirit that I, for one, have sought to improve the present Divorce Act.
I think that most proposals made for the commendable purpose of improving this bill implied some degree of provincial action, because almost all the solutions suggested concerned, either directly or indirectly, fields coming under provincial jurisdiction.
The government was faced with this dilemma: Should it wait several years before amending the Divorce Act, years which would be spent usefully negotiating with the provinces toward the setting up of a new system of courts, perhaps family courts as was suggested, which would have wide powers to act in the field of reconciliation? Should it still wait a long time to solve the very real problems of conflicting rights which this bill poses, and then perhaps, one, two or three years later introduce a bill, after rather complex negotiations, because they are related to constitutional matters, and members know that the constitution is not now an easy matter? Should the government wait for one year or perhaps several years to produce a bill closer to perfection, or should it act as soon as possible and attempt to introduce the best possible bill under our jurisdiction and let negotiations continue, as I have repeatedly indicated, at federal-provincial meetings, and undertake direct negotiations later which would eventually lead to improving the law?
We, on this side of the house, have decided in favour of a procedure which the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) considers perhaps a little too precipitous, a little too hurried, and which is certainly liberal rather than conservative with regard to the time factor.

In our opinion, the legislation we have prepared is quite within the jurisdiction of the federal government; we have gone as far as possible, and I suggest to the hon. members that they examine the bill and criticize it in that light.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)

The point I said I should like to deal with in a little bit of detail before going into greater detail when we reach the committee stage is the point of marriage breakdown. This concept or theory is a very progressive one and one to which I have not so much of a philosophical or moral objection but one in which I see real difficulties of a legal or constitutional order. Let me deal first with a matter of substance. I should say first, Mr. Speaker, that we have dealt with the marriage breakdown concept in a certain form. The bill itself speaks of breakdown and this is more than lip service. We are introducing the breakdown concept as one which is supplementary or additional to the concept of offences. This is a completely new approach in our law, of course.
As I say, it is not mere lip service and what we are attempting to do is to spell out the conditions under which the courts may or shall find there has been breakdown. When I listened to those members who objected to our approach discussing this problem it seemed to me that they always came back, in one way or another, to the type of legislation we have here. They would say that they favoured the breakdown approach, nothing more and nothing less. However, when called upon to spell it out in a little bit of detail they always indicated legislation giving the factors of the breakdown, giving some guidance to the court. For instance, I should like to refer to page 5484 of Hansard where I find the report of the eloquent speech made by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). He referred to a private bill introduced in the United Kingdom, not by the government, which has not yet reached any stage of implementation. He made a fairly good summary of the provisions of the bill and then said:
There will henceforth be only one ground for divorce in Britain.-proof that "the marriage has irretrievably broken down". This will be deemed to have happened:
(a)	If the parties have ceased to cohabit for two years-
We have this in our law but we have set it at three years. It may be too much and perhaps the period should be shorter. This is
December 18, 1967

a matter for discussion. We are now talking about the theoretical concept of breakdown and giving guidance to the courts. The bill the hon. member mentioned is a proposal which has not even reached the stage of legislation and is no improvement on ours. Once again, it is a question of time. We have three periods in our bill. We have the one year concept for non-consummation, we have two years for certain circumstances of imprisonment and we have three years for normal separation. We even have five years when there is desertion by the petitioner. These periods can be discussed and changed, but certainly the concept has been established in our bill.
The next ground is:
(b)	If the couple have ceased to cohabit for five years, even though one does not want divorce-
This is exactly our five year test in the case of desertion. Then, ground (c) reads:
(c)	If there is conduct which a husband or wife cannot be reasonably expected to endure, or adultery which either cannot after reflection forgive.
What is the great difference between this proposal in this revolutionary bill and ours? What is conduct which one party cannot endure or adultery which either cannot after reflection forgive? We have the adultery test. We have forgiveness in the sense there is a possibility of condonation. In so far as conduct which could not reasonably be expected to be endured is concerned, I cannot say what is meant. Surely our provision covering cruelty would, in most cases, cover this. I say that even those who propound their abstract theories, when they are called upon to spell out what they mean, in most cases adopt this type of answer.
Another illustration will be found at page 5500 of Hansard where a question asked by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brew-in) of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) is recorded. The hon. member for Broadview was indicating a certain preference at that point for the concept of divorce which is included in our bill. The question reads as follows:
Does he not see you could still have breakdown which would require separation for three years, if that was the sole reason for the action; but if there was the so-called outrageous conduct you could then say the marriage had broken down in a period less than three years.
Well, this is our test. If there were no reconciliation and if there were such outrageous conduct, then you could say the marriage had broken down in a period of less
Divorce Law Reform
than three years. Here again the phrase "outrageous conduct" is wide. What does it mean? This is a test the courts will have to meet one way or another. I am not convinced that even those who want to talk about the substance of this procedure are talking about anything very different, if I am to judge from these examples, from what we are doing.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Procedure is something else again. The breakdown of marriage concept which has been espoused from many quarters presupposes a complete change in our conception of courts and justice. I should like to read a few brief quotations in this connection, and I refer first to the excellent report of the special joint committee on divorce, page 116. I am not going to read as much as I would like, but this matter is dealt with very clearly in this passage:
The novelty of the marriage breakdown theory does not He simply in the grounds it proposes for dissolutions of marriage, but also in the procedure that would be required to effect the system. Indeed, it is not the essential vaUdity of the theory that seems to merit the most careful inspection at this stage, but the practical consequences that would flow from it, were it to be adopted.
The existing system for the trial of divorce cases based upon the adversary method, the traditional practice of our courts, whereby the judge is the arbiter between two contending parties, would have to be changed. The procedure would have to be that of an inquest or inquiry into the state of the marriage, if the marriage breakdown system were to work. The parties would not provide all the evidence and the court might have to seek out and introduce evidence of its own.
According to this quotation, Mr. Speaker, I think you would need to have a different concept of what is a court. Also required would be experts trained in social services and family matters to give evidence. This would involve questions such as the children of the marriage, how they would be cared for, what was the pre-existing situation, problems of delinquency and so on.
This gets back to the difficulty I referred to at the outset of my remarks, that we are embarking on certain areas that are under provincial jurisdiction. I suggest we would have to negotiate for some time with the provinces before being successful in setting up this type of court. As I have said, we took the attitude that we should act now and do the most we can under our present jurisdiction. We will improve the law as time goes on but we cannot refuse the obvious remedy of divorce in those cases that will be embraced under the terms of the bill as presently framed.

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
I should also like to cite a short extract from a report presented to the British parliament by the lord chancellor in November 1966, command paper 3123. I refer to the conclusions of the report, which are to be found at page 54 and sum up a very long argument set forth in the command paper:
The proposals of the Archbishop's Group on Divorce made in "Putting Asunder"-
This was the proposal of marriage breakdown.
-though they are to be welcomed for their rejection of exclusive reliance on matrimonial offence, are procedurally impracticable. They propose that there should be but one comprehensive ground for divorce-breakdown of the marriage- the court being required to satisfy itself by means of a thorough inquest into the marriage that it has failed irretrievably. It would not be feasible, even if it were desirable, to undertake such an inquest in every divorce case because of the time this would take and the costs involved.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, this is a mere summary of the argument. I cannot deal with it in detail though it has been excellently presented in the report. However, a few lines that appear on page 32 spell out the argument that is here summed up:
If the inquest was to become a genuine one-
I should like the hon. members who are so keen on the marriage breakdown concept to realize this point.
-preliminary enquiries by trained personnel would have to be undertaken and the actual hearing would have to take much longer than at present. Moreover, it seems to us that public opinion would be unlikely to regard it as an improvement if in every case the whole matrimonial history were ventilated in public. In effect, this would be to introduce into every divorce case the distressing features of defended divorces which at present constitute only about 7 per cent of the total. The Archbishop's Group appear to face this prospect with an equanimity that we cannot share. If our divorce laws are to be made more humane, it seems to us that the undefended divorce affords a better model than the dilatory, expensive and distressing defended divorce.

In his discussions of this matter has the minister considered the fact that the objection raised by the law commission in Great Britain to the necessity for an inquest in all cases on the law of breakdown would be met by a provision that after a period of separation, say three years or whatever it may be, there would then be a prima facie presumption of breakdown? If the law were to provide for this, the necessity for an

inquest or inquiry would be confined to those cases where there was some other ground that properly deserved investigation. Has the minister considered that point? If he reads the report of the law commission carefully he may find the suggestion that I am making to him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the type of point that I made a moment ago. By putting this three year test into the breakdown concept you are destroying the purity of the breakdown concept. We are making provision in the bill for evidence to be given to the courts which is indicative of breakdown. We are also avoiding the necessity for an inquest by giving the courts in some cases three years before finally settling the matter. Under clause 4 (1) (e) we are providing for a three-year test.
Under the proposition advanced by the hon. member the purity of the breakdown concept is destroyed, and, as I shall show in a moment by reference to the Archbishop's report, this is not desirable. The hon. member is suggesting a shortcut which is contrary to the spirit of those who support the breakdown concept. However, if he will be patient for a moment I should like to read an excerpt from "Putting Asunder" which expresses this argument exactly.
I also wanted to refer to a quotation from the London Times of May 8, 1967 where there is a fairly enlightening quotation from Lord Gardiner, but in view of the time factor I shall not read it. It is very much to the same effect, namely that the difficulty of marriage breakdown is procedural in nature. It is not the concept itself. It is the impossibility of writing it into our system of law as it presently exists. I should like to pass on to a few short quotations from the report entitled "Putting Asunder" prepared by a group appointed by the Archbishop of Canterbury in January, 1964. Those who are familiar with this report will realize that the marriage breakdown concept meets with the same difficulty in the United Kingdom as I am outlining now. This report contains a number of recommendations respecting the divorce courts, recommendations which are regarded as so necessary, and here I quote from page 76, "that we could not continue to support the principle of breakdown if they were not implemented in substance."
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
What are those recommendations, Mr. Speaker, which would have to be implemented and which, if not implemented, would
December 18, 1967

prevent the breakdown concept from being accepted? Quoting once again from page 76 of the report one finds the following:
(c)	that the accusatorial procedure should be replaced by procedure appropriate to inquiry into the condition of marriage relationships;
(d)	that means should be devised to ensure that all relevant information and conditions would be brought to the court's notice;
(e)	that steps should be taken without delay to enlist the officers the court would need.
The report then goes on to point out that an uncontested case could, on occasion, call for greater care and judicial skill than a case which was contested.
There is another part of this report to which I wish to refer, Mr. Speaker. I refer to appendix C, the second part of which consists of an essay written by Mr. Quentin Edwards, a barrister at law and one of the members of the group that was appointed by the Archbishop. The conclusions of Mr. Quentin Edwards which are expressed at the bottom of page 135 and on the following pages are that the whole constitution and procedure of the high court under existing statutes and rules create reasonable doubt whether the high court could, if the substantive law were changed as recommended, satisfy the requirements prescribed as necessary to administer the new law. His conclusions, as set out on page 136 of the report, are that serious consideration might well be given to establishing an entirely new system of courts.
There can, I think, be little doubt that the wholesale adoption of the marriage breakdown concept as advocated in the report "Putting Asunder" would necessarily require the creation of new matrimonial courts that would administer the new laws after a form and procedure quite different from our existing judicial institutions across this country. It would be necessary, for example, to have welfare officers, social workers and other officials attached to such courts to administer effectively the marriage breakdown concept.
I think it would also be necessary to have the judges of these courts specially trained in the field of matrimonial relations so that they would have a proper understanding of the dynamics of marriage and the causes of breakdown. The report is, for this reason, more visionary than real.
The appendix also sets out types of difficulties that we are not presently able to solve at the federal level of government under the constitution. In this instance, particularly, we were faced with this dilemma. Should we hold up divorce reform for X
Divorce Law Reform
number of years until we have written a new constitution and perhaps given the provinces jurisdiction over marriage and divorce problems or should we perhaps attempt with the provinces to deal with this matter which, remotely, or not remotely, so far as the administration of justice is concerned, comes under the federal government's jurisdiction? In the face of this dilemma we answered that we must act now under our jurisdiction and that we could not wait until the whole judicial system was reformed in order to satisfy those who, for very good, theoretical reasons, prefer the breakdown concept.
My argument is very much the same with respect to the reconciliation procedures contained in the bill. Admittedly, those procedures are not as far reaching and as thorough as many good meaning people would like to see. Personally I also regard reconciliation procedures as being most important. I can only say that I think we have gone as far as we can under this law. That is to say, we have gone as far as we can without embarking on a prolonged and involved process of federal-provincial consultation.
In saying that we adopted the procedure of acting now I want to add that I am not trying to minimize the importance of federal-provincial consultations. I, for one, would have preferred those consultations to have taken place 10 or 15 years ago or sooner. We would then have a system of courts-call them family courts, integrated family, marriage and divorce courts, or what you will- in which to apply the pure marriage breakdown theory. The fact is that we do not have these types of courts now. They would need to be set up, and that step can only be taken after long consultation with the provinces. I thought it preferable, and perhaps more in keeping with the will of the nation, to proceed with divorce reform as quickly as we could without, of course, neglecting any very important factors.

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to a return to adequate shipbuilding subsidies, and regional tendering and allocation of new construction, overhaul and repair.
He said: Mr. Speaker, first may I say it is a pleasure to take part in private members' hour. When a private member places one of these motions on the order paper he, of course, takes his chance on when it will be called, and I am glad that after some period of time the important matter with which my motion deals has now come before the house. If I may speak politically for a moment I wish to say that embodied in this motion is a resolution adopted by the Atlantic provinces Conservative candidates at a meeting in the city of Moncton, New Brunswick, and one which is most important to the Atlantic area.
I intend to divide my remarks into three sections, the first dealing with the matter of steel trawler construction in the Atlantic area. The building subsidies for steel fishing trawlers and other commercial ships were introduced in a policy brought forward by the previous government when the former hon. member for Trois-Rivieres was minister of transport. These subsidies have meant a lot to Canadian shipyards.
I recall going to the Canadian Maritime Commission, which is now part of the Canadian Transport Commission, and speaking with its chairman, Alex Watson, a man of
December 18, 1967

Scotch descent and naturally very durable, who had worked hard to have the subsidy scheme introduced and adopted by the previous government. For ordinary commercial vessels 40 per cent was the amount set as the percentage to be paid by the federal government and for steel fishing trawlers the amount was 50 per cent.
This program accomplished two things. It assisted our Canadian fishery companies to get up to date equipment in the form of new trawlers so that they could compete with foreign fishery trawlers off our coasts. Second and of no less importance, it provided the means whereby our shipbuilding yards could compete with foreign shipyards. Prior to its introduction our fishing companies, in most if not in all cases, bought their vessels from European shipyards where, because of the assistance given those yards by their respective governments, they could get their trawlers at a lower price than they would have had to pay in Canada.
As has been widely reported and commented upon, on the night of December 7 the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Benson) made the following announcement:
The 50 per cent subsidy now provided for the construction of steel hull fishing trawlers will be reduced to 35 per cent, effective tonight.
I wish to emphasize the suddenness with which this cut was made. I have looked into this matter and I am advised that a number of fishing companies were in the midst of negotiations with shipyards to have new vessels built when this announcement was made on December 7 and that the announcement may well mean the negotiations will end without any settlement, causing a terrific loss to the shipyards.
As reported in the New Glasgow News of December 11, one of the executives of Jerry Nickerson and Sons Ltd. stated:
The 15 per cent decrease in subsidy has given us two choices-build abroad or not build at all.
The Nova Scotia deputy minister of fisheries, Brian Meagher, was reported in the same newspaper as saying:
an average 150 foot trawler costs approximately $1,000,000, of which 50 per cent has been paid by subsidy. Its annual catch is valued between $250,000-$300,000 and it gives employment to 100 men ashore and 15-19 men afloat.
From this it will be seen that the construction of trawlers means not only work for our shipyards but also work for those engaged in our fisheries. The effect of the minister's announcement was too sudden.

I think that debate on the motion I have proposed comes at an opportune time, and I would urge the	government	to	reconsiderthe matter of subsidies on the construction of steel fishing trawlers. Not only should the applications for subsidy now in the hands of the Department	of	Industry	be	considered,
but there should have been a date set warning the shipyards and fishing companies that were engaged in negotiations when the subsidy was to be cut.
I wish to quote now part of an editorial which appeared	in	the Halifax	Chronicle-
Herald of December	14:
Perhaps the reduction-
The reduction in subsidies.
-is designed to show people in landlocked parts of the country that the maritimes have not escaped Mr. Benson's axe entirely. If retained for a prolonged period, however, it might have a most harmful effect on shipbuilding in the Atlantic provinces, which has already been hit by a slump in orders for both steel and wooden fishing vessels.
There is a danger that once demand for new construction and the replacement of existing vessels begins to pick up, the reduced subsidy will persuade fleet owners to look elsewhere for their vessels. Modern steel trawlers, suited to northwest Atlantic fishing operations, are being built in quantity in various countries. There are numbers of ways in which Nova Scotia and other Canadian buyers can obtain easy credit terms for these foreign-built ships.
It would be a serious matter for Canadian shipyards if foreign builders obtained a substantial toehold in this way. The price would be ridiculous: a meaningless federal bow to fiscal prudence.
In the first budget introduced by the present government the then minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), pointed out the number of millions of dollars which had gone into this project. It is money which I think was well spent. The subsidy was 40 per cent for ordinary commercial construction but now it has been cut to 25 per cent and will remain at that level until May 31, 1969. After May 31, 1969, it will be reduced still further by 2 per cent a year until it reaches 17 per cent. As a result construction of this type of vessel will decrease.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
Part of my motion, Mr. Speaker, deals with regional tendering. I believe there should be regional tendering, but the government has adopted a policy of national tendering. I remember the time a few years ago when tenders were called for the first coastguard vessels. I recall that the low bidders were two St. Lawrence river yards. The lowest bidder in the Atlantic area at that time-and this shows that regional tendering could

help-was a shipyard in my own constituency, Ferguson Industries Limited. I went to the minister of fisheries at that time, the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, and put forward a proposition to assist employment in Canada. I proposed that two of the contracts should go to the St. Lawrence river yards and the third should go to the yard in my constituency since it was the lowest of the Atlantic area bidders. I can think also of the case of the ferry plying between Portugal Cove and Bell Island, Newfoundland, the John Guy. Regional tendering was permitted in this case and as a result the shipyard in my constituency obtained the contract. This system gives not only the major yards but particularly the smaller yards an opportunity to tender and thereby keep the shipyards employed.
Certainly in my area and most areas during the last few years there has been very little naval repair work given out in the form of contracts because the number of ships has been cut down. In my own area, with the exception of one or two very small contracts in amounts under $25,000 nothing has been done in that regard in the last three years. I believe that naval work could be allocated to these yards. I am not sure whether this practice is carried on now, but the Department of Defence Production had a system whereby they would put a ship into a shipyard and if the management could do a good job and finish the contract before a designated time a bonus was given based on a bonus system. I believe this was a good thing.
I do not wish to take up too much time because I believe other members wish to speak on this matter. The most important point is that there should be a return to the subsidies. As I say, I hope the government will look into the matter of returning to the former subsidies in respect of the construction of steel fishing trawlers. If we do not return to the former system. I am afraid, as pointed out by the executive of Jerry Nickerson and Sons Ltd., that the ships either will be built abroad or not at all. If they are built abroad it will mean that foreign companies will be building our ships and will have their foot in the door. This will be fatal to our shipyards.
Shipyards are necessary not only in peacetime but also in wartime. We must keep them active in peacetime in order to provide the necessary work and employment and so that in the event of war they will be ready to deal with matters of national concern. We do not want to be left without our shipyards. I
[Mr. MacEwan.l
think the shipbuilding subsidies program is what has helped put our shipyards on their feet. A decrease in the subsidy or the taking away of the subsidy would have the reverse effect. I should like to refer again to _ the article which appeared in the Chronicle-Herald of December 14:
It would be a serious matter for Canadian shipyards if foreign builders obtained a substantial toehold in this way. The price would be ridiculous: a meaningless federal bow to fiscal prudence.
The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud), in answering a question I asked the other day, pointed out that the amounts which had been paid out were $24 million for steel vessels and over $6 million for wooden vessels for the fisheries. All I can say is that I hope this resolution will come to a vote and pass and that the government will give consideration to the meaningless cuts they have brought about. If money was spent it was money well spent.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the great advantages of private members' hour is that it provides an opportunity for us to air our opinions on matters of concern to our ridings. I think there are very few members in the house who are more concerned about shipbuilding than myself. Like my colleague and friend from Pictou I have in my riding, as it is now constituted, some shipbuilding facilities. There are two major shipyards, one large H.M.C. Dockyard at Esquimalt, and one medium size shipyard which specializes in building certain types of craft. Unfortunately, one of the major shipyards is in the process of scrapping its shipbuilding facilities. It is remaining in the steel fabricating part of the business. This is a result of the present state of affairs in the country.
I think one of the troubles in Canada at the moment is that while we have a government ship procurement policy and hand in hand with it have a shipbuilding subsidy program, we do not have a maritime shipping policy. It seems to me that the two should in fact go hand in hand if we wish to be honest and sincere about this whole matter. There does not seem to me to be any point in building ships purely for the sake of providing employment. This costs money in very large quantities and there may be better ways to provide employment.
In Canada with our population I do not think we can keep a large shipbuilding industry going on government contracts and subsidies alone. I believe we must become
December 18, 1967

competitive in world markets. We must build for the world. I think we can do that. We did at one time have a massive shipbuilding industry. Our achievement in wartime was simply magnificent. I wonder how many hon. members realize how stupendous it was. For example, I do not think there is a member in the house who is not aware of the fact that the Clyde river and Clydebank in Scotland are a huge shipbuilding area. In the port of Vancouver during world war II a larger tonnage of shipbuilding was turned out than was turned out in the whole of the Clyde river area. That is a remarkable achievement. Of course, with the peacetime cut-backs construction has diminished so that at the moment on the west coast, for example, we have remaining two large shipbuilding facilities and various shipbuilding organizations of a smaller nature.
As I said, we do not have a national shipbuilding policy. We have a policy of ship procurement which to my mind is on trial. The present situation is that the government, for the first time, has lumped together all its shipbuilding requirements whether they be for the Department of National Defence or for another government department. They have stated what their requirements are to be. They have forecast these over a period of years and have given this information to the shipbuilding industry across Canada so that these yards now know that when times are tough and they need extra work they can sharpen their pencils and become really competitive.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I went along and do go along with this government policy and I think we must at least try it out to see if it will work. There have been many signs that we can compete on the west coast, in spite of our higher wage rates, with shipbuilding yards on the east coast of Canada. I do not have the figures in this regard at my fingertips but I will come back to this point later. In the United States the situation is different. As I said earlier, we should not only have a ship procurement but a maritime shipping policy. They do have one in the United States and I think it is called the Jones Act. Their declaration of policy reads in this way and I quote from subsection 1101:
It is necessary for the national defence and development of its foreign and domestic commerce that the United States shall have a merchant marine (a) sufficient to carry its domestic waterborne commerce and a substantial portion of the water-borne export and import foreign commerce of the United States and to provide shipping
Shipbuilding
service on all routes essential for maintaining the flow of such domestic and foreign water-borne commerce at all times, (b) capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency, (c) owned and operated under the United States flag by citizens of the United States, in so far as may be practicable, and (d) composed of the best-equipped, safest, and most suitable types of vessels, constructed in the United States and manned with a trained and efficient citizen personnel.
It goes on to state:
It is declared to be the policy of the United States to foster the development and encourage the maintenance of such a merchant marine.
That is what the Jones Act says. The policy is clear, concise and desirable, but I think experience has shown that it is also expensive. I could read a few more provisions which have been developed over the years as they have gained experience. For instance, they have a construction differential subsidy. It is one of the things that followed the establishment of a national maritime policy. This subsection reads:
Any citizen of the United States may make application to the federal maritime board for a construction differential subsidy to aid in the construction of a new vessel to be used in the foreign commerce of the United States. No such application shall be approved by the board unless it determines that (1) the plans and specifications call for a new vessel which will meet the requirements of the foreign commerce of the United States, will aid in the promotion and development of such commerce and be suitable for use by the United States for national defence or military purposes in time of war or national emergency;-
It then states that the board must also determine that:
-the applicant possesses the ability, the experience, financial resources, and other qualifications necessary to enable it to operate and maintain the proposed new vessel, and (3) the granting of the aid applied for is reasonably calculated to replace worn out or obsolete tonnage with new and modem ships, or otherwise to carry out effectively the purposes and policy of this chapter.
I will not go farther with that point, but they have a maritime policy from which flows the requirement for a construction subsidy. There is also the important fact that if you are going to have a maritime policy and build ships you ought to have the facilities for building the ships. In the next paragraph it is stated:
The federal maritime board shall submit the plans and specifications for the proposed vessel to the navy department for examination thereof and suggestions for such changes therein as may be deemed necessary or proper in order that such vessel shall be suitable for economic and speedy conversion into a naval or military auxiliary, or otherwise suitable for the use of the United States government in time of war or national emergency.

In order to make the policy economical it then goes on to say:
All licensed officers of vessels documented under the laws of the United States, as now required by law, shall be citizens of the United States, native born or completely naturalized; and upon each departure from the United States of a cargo vessel in respect of which a construction or operating subsidy has been granted all of the crew (crew including all employees of the ship) shall be citizens of the United States, native born or completely naturalized.
I am trying to show how complicated this matter becomes. It then says, and this will be of help to hon. members who were talking about this before-you will be happy to hear that I seem to have lost my place.

To make this an economically viable operation the act states:
Any officer or employee of the United States travelling on official business ... shall travel and transport his personal effects on ships registered under the laws of the United States-
It then goes on to state:
Whenever the United States shall procure, contract for, or otherwise obtain for its own account, or shall furnish to or for the account of any foreign nation without provision for reimbursement, any equipment, materials, or commodities, within or without the United States, or shall advance funds or credits or guarantee the convertibility of foreign currencies in connection with the furnishing of such equipment, materials, or commodities, the appropriate agency or agencies shall take such steps as may be necessary and practicable to assure that at least 50 per centum of the gross tonnage of such equipment, materials or commodities .. . shall be transported on privately owned United States flag commercial vessels-
I read this to show that the problem in respect of providing subsidies to the shipbuilding industry in Canada is not simple. To spare hon. members on all sides of the house I have only read parts of the law. I have here an extract from a Seattle newspaper which gives a fairly good idea of how this policy is working in the United States. The article refers to how the Jones Act applies to people in Alaska and it states:
Rightly or wrongly, many Alaskans see those laws-"Jones" or "inter-coastal"-whatever you prefer-as slowing the northland's development because they in effect limit competition and raise the cost of shipping.
As they stand now, those laws outlaw shipping of U.S. goods between two U.S. ports in a foreign vessel. A vessel qualifies as "foreign" if it wasn't built in a U.S. shipyard.
Later it states:
Alaska just recently put on the heat in the U.S. Congress to permit the shipment of goods on Canadian ferries en route from here to Alaska but the measure was defeated.

The coastal shipping laws, as far as the rest of the economy here is concerned, have done their work too well. For one thing costs are higher on the U.S. vessels. Put those two facts together and it practically meant the death knell for the regions water-borne shipment of lumber to the U.S. east coast.
Let me point out this fact, however, still quoting from this article:
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
Lumber from British Columbia, however, has all but taken that market away from our region's producers. During the month of October, for instance, British Columbia sent 64.8 million board feet of lumber to the east coast via ship; Washington-
Another lumber state.
-7 million; Oregon, 11.3 million.
The difference doesn't turn on the quality of our lumber or the price here.
That is one example. You lose trade when you try to confine the shipment or your own materials to your own ships. I think another example that we all remember is the United States wheat sales last year to China. Because of the requirement by the government of that country that half of those wheat sales would have to be shipped in American bottoms, the cost of the wheat to the Chinese was increased so that they were no longer agreeable to buying it from the United States. The United States suffered; we were the ones who benefited.
This notice of motion calls for adequate shipbuilding subsidies. I think this is a little vague. I am not too sure what "adequate" means. I would have preferred the language to be a little more definite. How is our present system working? Some rather interesting figures came to light only yesterday. I refer to a press release issued by the Department of Defence Production, dated December 12, which says:
Shortly after 3.00 p.m. today, proposals for the construction and outfitting of the four helicoptercarrying destroyers (d.d.h. 280 class) were opened publicly by officials of the Department of Defence Production with the results as indicated in Appendix A.
Appendix A shows that for the lead yards two firms, Davie Shipbuilding Ltd. and Marine Industries Ltd., bid on the construction of the lead ship and one other. The indicated price for Davie is just over $24 million and for Marine Industries it is about $20.5 million.
For the follow-up yards, two more ships, Marine Industries came up with a bid of just about $18.5 million, Davie Shipbuilding came
December 18, 1967



up with a bid of $22.5 million, Halifax Shipyards, that is Dosco, came up with a bid of just under $35 million and Burrard Dry Dock, in North Vancouver, came up with a bid of just over $49 million. This looks pretty bad for the west coast, but what it suggests to me is not that regional tendering is the answer but, as I am beginning to suspect, that the method of tendering needs looking into. There cannot be a spread of $31 million between the east coast and the west coast in respect of bids for identical ships.
On the west coast we have a wage differential of 70 cents an hour, or about a dollar an hour with fringe benefits; but the difference in wages is not $31 million. To my mind there is something wrong with the way those tenders were worded. There must have been too many vaguely worded clauses in the tenders which allowed for different interpretations between the east coast and the west coast, and the interpretation given on the west coast called for a far more expensive construction. I shall be very interested to see what is the final cost of these ships when construction is completed.
I am just about finished, Mr. Speaker. I want to see a shipbuilidng and repair facility kept on both coasts of Canada. If we are to be a maritime nation we must not only build ships but repair them on both coasts. I think there are ways of doing this other than by means of direct subsidy. I believe the shipyards have shown commendable activity and skill in diversifying and becoming steel fabricators, and in imaginative ship construction projects. They have developed in my own area some very highly skilled procedures in the building of offshore oil drilling rigs. I want to see this sort of activity continued.
I think there is a very large field for Canada contributing through external aid in the building of shipping; and shipping, of course, involves not just ships and offshore oil-drilling rigs but all sorts of other types of steel fabricating. I see that my time is just about up, Mr. Speaker. I wish to deal at another time with a scheme I have of trying to develop in Canada, using our external aid program, a school of harbour development by means of which we can use our shipbuilding facilities and talents as part of the contribution to our external aid program. However, as I say, I will do that at another time.

In the constituency represented by my colleague and myself we have the Halifax Shipyards. We have been told in discussions with officials of Halifax Shipyards-and this is also a matter of public record-that they

consider the fishing industry to be the greatest source of work for these yards. As most people who know the Halifax area will realize, the shipyards lie alongside the dockyard and alongside what is left of the Royal Canadian Navy, and yet these officials told us that the shipyard potential is in the fishing industry, and not in naval construction or naval refits. So instead of being able to take steps to offset the effects of the devaluation of the British pound and to adjust to that situation, we have taken steps which go hand in hand with the devaluation, but to the detriment of Canadian industry. We were met with various suggestions, that the work should be done on tender call, and the like. However, let us ask ourselves: if we have ever set up this type of industry on an economic basis in this country. I suggest we did not because if we had done so the yards on the St. Lawrence river and those on the west and east coasts would never have been asked to tender on the D.D.P. program. Perhaps the tenders would have gone overseas, or around the world to places where these ships can be built on a much lower wage scale and at a much lower price than in Canada.
So we have to admit that our defence contracts are partly used as an economic development weapon. Once we admit this, we must also admit that the various regions in Canada must be treated equitably. We have the west coast, where obviously the wage differential in comparison with the Atlantic and east coast yards puts them out of the picture. Then there is the St. Lawrence river, where another set of economic conditions prevails; and finally there is Atlantic Canada, the area I serve, where still other economic factors are at work. So if we grant that defence spending is a necessary economic weapon in the hands of Canadians, then perforce we must grant that it cannot be applied in the way in which the government is presently applying it, a policy with regard to which my hon. friend for Pictou (Mr. Mac-Ewan) is seeking an answer. I think it is an important point.

Firm after firm from the Halifax area has written to me complaining that when the D.D.P. tenders were called they could not attempt to put any in because the vicious l.c.l. rates 
increased their prices so much that competition simply became impossible. I make this point because the Atlantic resolutions, to which my hon. friend referred, will be brought up again after the next election to save the day for the hard pressed Atlantic industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to deal with a couple of points with regard to the motion before the house which deals with the building of vessels in general, and fishing vessels in particular. A remark was made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. MacEwan) which perhaps should be challenged, that is that the reduction of subsidies for shipyards was made suddenly and that they were not prepared for it. I am given to understand by the government that the shipyards were warned a year ago of the impending reductions. They were informed that no subsidies would be granted under the existing rates for work that could not be completed within two years. So apparently they were aware of the impending reductions in the subsidy.
I believe it would be useful to give the house an idea of the size of the subsidy and what it has meant to the industry. For example, $24 million will be paid for steel hulls this year, and the Department of Fisheries, under its wooden ship construction program, will put out another $6J million, which makes a total of $30J million in subsidies granted to the shipyards for both steel and wooden hulls in the course of the current year. This subsidy has been granted for a number of years, and in the course of its history it has proved the capability of yards to turn out ships. Surely the capability of yards on both the east and the west coast must have improved as a result of the number of ships built under the subsidy. I think one of the direct benefits to the Canadian shipbuilding industry has been the fact that the subsidy has enabled them to improve their capital equipment and to build up a capability for meeting the very kind of competition for which it was designed.
Bearing this in mind, I think we should look at the money that we as the government have put out in subsidies, and ask ourselves just how we propose to handle this. Does a subsidy have to be continued indefinitely, and must it be repeated year after year, or is it possible that the government can put out money, as it has in shipbuilding programs, to encourage shipbuilding yards to improve their capability and meet their competition.

and finally to reduce the amount of subsidy and turn government funds to some other purposes?

speechtext:
I do not think it is a case of determining to what better use money could be put. One way of dealing with the matter would be simply not too levy the tax. If it is possible with less subsidy to enable the shipbuilding industry to stand on its own feet, then surely as legislators we should strive for a position in which the ship building industry could operate on a smaller subsidy per hull, if it is possible to reduce the amount of subsidy granted to the industry. When the hon. member asks to what better purpose the money could be put, I say it might be turned back to the people to be used at their own discretion. We are often told by hon. members on the other side that we overspend. Perhaps money granted to this industry has now served its pupose to encourage the shipbuilding industry to a point where it can meet some competition.
I am glad to see in the house this afternoon the hon. member for Queens-Lunen-burg (Mr. Crouse) because when he and I served together on the fisheries committee it was he who raised the question of the Golden Scarab, a Canadian subsidized vessel which was built in Canadian shipyards and which I am sure the government, in providing money for the building of that and similar ships, expected would ship in Canadian waters, hire Canadian crews, come back to Canadian docks and send its fish to Canadian markets, thus benefiting the economy of Canada. But as he explained so well to the committee, this was not what happened. Indeed the Golden Scarab disappeared from the Canadian scene. It fished in foreign waters, took on foreign crews and landed its catch in foreign ports for processing. This vessel therefore was literally lost to the Canadian economy after it had been built here.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
We recommended, and my hon. friend was a party to that recommendation, that the
Shipbuilding
Canadian government should tighten up the policing of subsidies of this kind, and that there should be in the subsidy more than merely the provision of funds to assist in the building of a hull. We should make sure that the hull will remain useful to the Canadian economy beyond the date of its launching. This motion suggests that the government should give immediate consideration to a return to adequate shipbuilding subsidies. I think one of the things we should make sure about is that the funds we provide do not simply build hulls, but that those hulls continue to perform a useful service to the Canadian economy.
It is not only in connection with the building of fishing vessels that such situations crop up, but they occur everywhere in connection with vessel construction under the Canadian subsidy system. I have in my hand a copy of the Appropriations Act, which includes the regulations in respect of capital subsidies for the construction of commercial fishing vessels. The definition of shipowner is a citizen of Canada, a company incorporated in Canada or Her Majesty in the right of any province in Canada. Under this definition, then, any foreign company which wants to take advantage of this Canadian subsidy can come to Canada and incorporate itself or gain control of a Canadian company already established. Such a company could then use the dollars which are obtained by virtue of the subsidy as leverage for acquiring an interest in a Canadian shipping company.
We had one famous example of this on the west coast. A locally owned tugboat company became owned by a United States company from New York. The United States company then provided the funds necessary for the building of vessels under the subsidy. The vessels were built in Canada and the Canadian government paid for the building of these vessels for this United States owned company. These vessels then went into competition on the Georgia strait with vessels of Canadian owned companies operating in those waters. These Canadian funds, raised from Canadian taxpayers, were made available to a United States company through the device of the subsidy, and were used as leverage to acquire an interest in a Canadian firm. The vessels were used in competition with those owned by Canadian companies.
I believe we should consider very carefully this aspect of the question of shipbuilding subsidies. I have raised this issue before in the House of Commons, and I raise it again

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
tonight because I really believe that the funds are not being put to the best use. In the case of the Golden Scarab, these funds were used to build a ship which sailed off into foreign waters. In the second case, the funds were used as leverage by a foreign company to acquire a Canadian company and to go into competition against Canadian companies. I believe these subsidies should be made available to Canadian firms, and they should not be capable of being used as leverage by companies from other countries.
I could give other examples. There are many barges operating in the Georgia strait carrying wood chips and paper. More and more these barges have come to be built and operated by the pulp and paper companies on the west coast. At one time they were operated by locally owned shipping firms which operated up and down the strait. However, the availability of these subsidies has meant that pulp and paper companies owned and operated in the United States have found it profitable to use this Canadian subsidy to build barges for use in that area.
So I ask, does anyone in this house really feel we are putting this money to good use when it is being used as leverage funds for the purpose of assisting United States based pulp and paper companies operating in Canada? I feel this resolution should have added to it some clause which would enable us to look into these aspects of subsidies, as well as the other questions which have been raised by hon. members opposite.

I say, the theoretically pure concept of breakdown for which some hon. members have been pushing. I just want to wind up by spelling out in a little detail the kind of procedural change that would be required by the introduction of a concept which made several eminent British spokesmen declare- and this was referred to by the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on divorce-would be foreign to British law, and therefore I take it would also be foreign to Canadian law.
It is not so much the word "inquisitorial" that is distasteful; it is the practical difficulty of giving over to administrative boards or tribunals a type of decision which under our concept we give to the courts as part of the rule of law. A thorough application of this breakdown concept would really mean that we would authorize some kind of board or administrative tribunal-I am not quite sure what kind it would be; hon. members who spoke on the breakdown concept did not detail what they envisaged-which would have absolute or quasi-absolute discretion to inquire into all aspects of a marriage, and then reach a decision on standards which are the board's own and which were not tested by any text of law. Any decision of an administrative board could be appealed, only with great difficulty, because it would really mean substituting one administrative discretion for another.
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think it is closer to our concept of the rule of law for judicial tribunals or courts to apply the law, as we see it, and not for boards to inquire or pry into the very intimate aspects of the lives of the parties to a divorce suit. I think this law is a good one in the sense that the facts presented to the court spell out what is the state of marriage breakdown, and the court must accept those facts.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I feel that the procedure adopted in this bill is the best one. As I indicated earlier, it is the only one we could implement now without going through the very long procedure of reforming our judicial system.

For those reasons we-
"We" being the authors of this report,
-cannot approve bringing uncontested cases into the jurisdiction of the county courts. We find ourselves in agreement, as did the Morton commission and the Denning committee, with the words of the Gorell commission of 1912.
Then follows a quote from the Gorell commission:
-the gravity of divorce and other matrimonial cases, affecting as they do the family life, the status of the parties, the interests of their children, and the interest of the State in the moral and social well-being of its citizens, makes it desirable to provide, if possible, that, even for the poorest persons, these cases should be determined by the superior courts of the country assisted by the attendance of the bar, which we regard as of high importance in divorce and matrimonial cases, both in the interests of the parties and in the public interest.
That is the end of the quotation from the Gorell commission. I continue quoting from page 78 of "Putting Asunder".
We also fear that transfer of divorce jurisdiction to the county courts could have the effect of impeding more radical reforms that eventually might be seen to be desirable.
The point here is that, traditionally, the superior or high courts have always been regarded as having jurisdiction in matrimonial cases. The principles which are contained in the new divorce bill change many of the laws which have been applied by many of our courts for many years. There are in excess of 80 county and district courts in Canada, a substantial majority of them being in Ontario. There are none in the territories or in the province of Quebec. Incidentally, the province of Quebec does not have county courts. All Quebec judges are judges of the superior courts and as such fulfil the role of county judges. Therefore in Quebec and in the territories, the kind of objection that has been raised does not apply.
It might be appropriate to indicate that each provincial legislature, if it so desires, can provide that county court judges shall act as local judges of the supreme court. Each province, if it so desires, could meet the objection which has been raised as to distance or as to the unattainability of superior courts. Each province must decide this matter in the light of its own problems as they arise in the administration of justice for that province.

I was arguing, Mr. Speaker, that the supreme court or high court is the natural court to render decisions in these types of matters. It seemed unwise to change our procedures radically. It seemed unwise to change the functions of courts at the same time as the substantive law is being changed.

In addition, to confer jurisdiction on the county courts would necessarily involve the inclusion of some principle that would enable a selection among those courts to be made. I am simply suggesting that that would be another factor that would have to be considered.
The hon. member raised the question of costs. That question is important, but I just wish to say this. Superior courts or supreme courts are not necessarily more expensive than county courts. Surely this is a matter which will be decided and fixed by the rules of courts, or by the code of civil procedure. I was hoping that this type of matter might be discussed in the meetings with the chief justices, meetings to which I referred a few minutes ago. Though the question of costs is important I do not think we should assume that necessarily it will be more expensive to litigate in supreme or high courts.
As a federal government we were dealing with effectively. Problems of legal aid, as with all aspects of the matter. Some aspects, however, the federal government, cannot cope hon. members know, cannot be solved by federal government action alone. At least, those problems can be solved only with great difficulty, if at all, where the federal government acts alone. Problems to do with lawyers' fees cannot be solved by the federal government, and court costs are fixed by rules.
Clause 19(1)(c) of the bill provides:
A court of appeal may make rules ...
(c) respecting the fixing and awarding of costs;
Subclause (2) provides:
-the governor in council may make such regulations as he considers proper to assure uniformity in the rules of court

We have therefore some leverage in this matter. I can only suggest that this type of question ought to be settled by provincial consultation. Again therefore we did not find it advisable to give jurisdiction to courts which seemed traditionally unprepared to decide these very substantial matters of rights, merely because costs were to be involved. That matter could be settled by another approach. In other words, here again we did not try to deal with everything in this bill. We have tried to draft the bill as best we could according to the powers we have.

It is obvious that the present divorce legislation, which is perfectly along the lines of the constitution, may, as a result, affect some other existing statutes under the Criminal Code. Here again, we have not felt that the decision to vote on a divorce legislation should be postponed indefinitely, nor deemed it necessary to wait until all legal conflicts are settled beforehand. I think it would have implied lengthy negotiations, and I am even inclined to say, very lengthy.
We have preferred to pass the legislation and keep strictly to questions of federal jurisdiction with the idea that later the courts will try to solve the problems of conflicting legislation under the principles applicable to other conflicting legislation throughout the country.
As for the question of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Laflamme) concerning children, I should simply indicate that the children over 16 will keep the rights they now have under the Civil Code. The present legislation deals with decisions rendered for children under 16, but the fact remains that section 165 and following clauses of the Civil Code dealing with alimony are not deleted for all that. These clauses apply to filiation and it is clear that the divorce legislation which breaks the bonds of matrimony cannot in the least break the bonds of filiation. Therefore, it may be that a 20-year-old son, wishing to pursue certain studies, may avail himself of the Quebec jurisprudence to the effect that he still has a claim on his father, regardless of the fact that the latter is divorced. Mr. Chairman, I propose to move an amendment to clause 2 to give divorce jurisdiction to the county and district courts. I shall give my reasons very briefly because the matter has been very carefully canvassed by members during debate on second reading, and a reply has been given by the minister. I think that the key to the success of this legislation lies in the question of jurisdiction. In the first place, high courts mean high costs. Divorce should not be the privilege of those who can afford it, but rather the right of those who merit it.
Second, divorce in the assize courts means divorce in a hurry. This has been one of the complaints over the years about divorce litigation, that it was shoved in without proper consideration, to be taken care of during proceedings in the assize courts at times when the judges had many other things on their minds. A very simple amendment to the bill could take care of this objection.
Third, reconciliation proceedings require continuing effort. In most areas county court judges are able to adjourn from time to time in order to follow up on reconciliation efforts. The high court judges are not. If these reconciliation proceedings, which some of us feel are unsatisfactory anyway, are to be at least carried out with some appearance of reality, then they should be carried out by judges who are able to continue their consideration of the matters involved.
These are the three points I want to raise. They were raised originally when I spoke on second reading, and I think they are still valid.
I would like to say a word about the minister's reply, because he made two or three points which had not been brought out previously. The first is that the provinces can now designate their local judges, who are county and district court judges, to try divorce actions. All I can say is that this power has been there all along, but it has never been used, except in Nova Scotia as my hon. friend from Pictou tells me. In general, across the country, this power has not been

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
used and there is no reason to think the new law will result in any changes unless there is some direction. Therefore I do not think that point is valid. If the law has been there in the past, this bill will make no change in that respect.
The minister also mentioned that the regulations as to costs could be made by the committee which sets up rules of court in each province. Here again I say that such committees could have done this all along. They could have made provision to make divorces less costly. If it is the intention to make them less costly, I am sure these committees would expect parliament to give them some lead; but we are giving them no lead in this legislation-except what may be gleamed from the debate on it, and the vote which we shall have now-to show that parliament really intends that the costs should be kept down. So while the minister made a number of good points, I really think that it is fundamental to grant divorce jurisdiction to the county and district courts.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Over the week end I have become even more completely convinced of this, since so many people have said that the purpose of this legislation, as expressed during the committee meetings and here, is to get away from the practice of having so many common law unions-I will not call them marriages, because they are not-which result in illegitimate children and in a negation of the sanctity of marriage itself. This is the purpose of this legislation.
In the first few months or years we would hope that many of these unsatisfactory unions would be made legal. This would be done by a party obtaining a divorce from his or her spouse, who lives somewhere else, and marrying the person with whom he or she is living. If this procedure is to cost a substantial sum of money, then it will not happen. These people, many of whom are unable to obtain a divorce because they cannot afford it, will be in no better position after this legislation has passed than they were before. So we will end up with a person who can afford a divorce getting it more easily on broader grounds while those on marginal incomes who would be unable, or would not have the desire, to raise several hundred dollars to obtain divorces in the high courts will more likely abandon the idea and buy new refrigerators or washing machines for their homesteads, rather than get divorces. This is a real possibility under any circumstance.

If this legislation does nothing more than broaden the grounds for those who can afford a divorce, then it will not help the situation. I believe we will find that the very objectives which I know the minister and the government have will go by the board unless this parliament directs that the county court judges are intended to be the judges who will preside over these trials. Unless this parliament directs that the costs shall be kept to a minimum, then I am sure the desired objective will not be achieved. If reconciliation proceedings are intended to be real, this will be more difficult and will shove up the costs unless there is jurisdiction in the county courts. County court costs are known to be generally less costly, regardless of how one looks at it. They will keep the costs down to a reasonable amount; they could be kept very low.
For all these reasons I urge very strongly that the minister reconsider this question of jurisdiction. I will pass up all my other objections if this one suggestion is accepted, because I believe the rest will all come together. In respect of the marriage breakdown, the minister has moved in that direction. He has not moved as far as some of us would like to see him move, but he has moved. On the question of reconciliation he has moved, perhaps not as far as we would like to see him move, but there is the seed of a move toward reconciliation procedures. On the matter of the county court jurisdiction, however, there is no movement at all. In fact, if it is resisted here, then it can be taken that the intention is to keep the jurisdiction with the high courts, keep the costs up, and not to reduce the costs. I would ask that the minister consider this question of the other courts, because I believe this is fundamental.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in order to give effect to this I have an amendment which I should like to propose. I might say that this is an amendment in which all our members on this side concur, even though we have some differences of opinion in respect of the marriage breakdown question and how far it should go. We are in agreement that the county court jurisdiction should have effect. We have taken clause 8 out of the draft bill proposed by the joint standing committee, and we would like to see it included in the bill which has been proposed by the minister. I, therefore, move:
That subclause (e) of clause 2 be amended by adding at the end thereof the following:
"(vii) In any province with courts having jurisdiction to dissolve marriages, the county or

district courts shall have jurisdiction, equally and concurrently with the superior court therein, to dissolve marriages and to provide ancillary relief, on any existing ground or on any ground added by this act: Provided that, on the application of any party thereto, an action for dissolution commenced in a county or district court shall be transferred to the superior court, and provided further that any ancillary relief granted by the superior court coincidentally with a pronouncement of dissolution may be enforced, and may be varied from time to time as circumstances may require, by the county or district court in the county or district in which the petitioner resides."

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Muskoka-Parry Sound. I shall try to make my remarks brief, because this matter has been discussed previously. There are some differences I have with the minister which I do not think can be very easily resolved and, although I may move or support amendments, I do not expect to persuade the minister. However, on this particular point concerning the jurisdiction of the county courts, once again I urge the minister to give consideration to this amendment.
There are a number of reasons. First I should like to refer to the report that was made by a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate. The members of this committee included a great many lawyers who are experienced in this field, including some from the Senate such as Senators Roebuck and Croll, for example. In addition, many hon. members on the government side of the house endorsed this report.
Divorce Law Reform
The report contained a unanimous recommendation that the jurisdiction be a concurrent jurisdiction in the county courts, and the reasons therefore are set out in the report. Although I do not propose to read this at any length, I should like to read the following which appears at page 261 of the appendix to Votes and Proceedings of June 27, 1967:
It is the practice in those provinces where dissolutions of marriage are granted for jurisdiction to be exercised by the superior courts. This practice has obvious disadvantages. The procedure of the superior courts is costly and involved, and these courts, burdened with cases of a more weighty character, tend to dispose of their long lists of divorce cases as quickly as possible and in a perfunctory manner.
I suggest that the voice of experience was speaking when that statement was made and that it is a fair statement of fact. I should like to read further from the report of the committee:
It would seem a far better solution-
And they have dealt with the idea of the family courts.
-to vest in the county courts concurrent jurisdiction with the supreme courts.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
These courts have advantages over the superior courts for the disposal of local divorce cases. Their procedure is less involved and consequently less costly. County court judges are resident in county towns and their local offices and officials are readily available at all times. The judges can be easily reached when an order needs to be explained or varied and when additional provisions are required. Furthermore, county court judges are more familiar with the local circumstances and situation, as well as being more accessible, and consequently are in a better position to make helpful judgments.
These remarks were not just those of any individual speaking; they are the remarks of a whole group of experienced lawyers and other members on the committee, both from the Senate and from the House of Commons, who heard the evidence and looked into this matter and came to this serious conclusion. I think it is up to the minister to give a little better answer as to who advised him to change this particular conclusion. I want to assure him that the points made here are correct. County court judges are accessible in various parts of the country, and I think particularly of the province of Ontario. I ask the minister to consult the lawyers in his own party in this house, who have had experience in these matters. They will repeat exactly what I am saying at this particular time.
The minister sweeps aside lightly the question of costs, and I do not think it should be

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
swept aside that lightly. The costs that are involved in this matter are going to be substantially lower in the county courts than they are in the supreme or superior courts. I cannot set an exact figure on this, but I suggest the difference lies somewhere between $200 or $300 for the average case in the county court, particularly if it is not opposed and there is a brief trial, and $600, $700 or $800 in the supreme court, again assuming that there is not a long trial. So we have the possibility here of cutting in half the costs, to litigants. Having this opportunity to cut this cost in half, why do we not avail ourselves of it by accepting that improvement which is recommended to us by the committee?
There is a lot more than this, and in respect of this matter I think the best witness we had before the committee, and I am a little prejudiced because he was a former partner of mine, was Mr. Justice McRuer, formerly chief justice of the high court of Ontario. In giving evidence before us he said this:
Jurisdiction in regard to divorce is in the superior courts, in the supreme court of Ontario. Jurisdiction in regard to custody may be with the surrogate court, which is the county court judge, the supreme court judge, or it may be that a family court judge can make an order for custody.
He then said:
I always felt awfully helpless in deciding a question of custody as a supreme court judge. I was very remote. I would go to Welland, and I would probably not be back in Welland again for five, six, or seven years. It is the same with other judges. We go on circuit, we go in and hear a case and we feel that we are not at the bottom of it at all, but we make an order for custody.
This evidence can be found in the proceedings of the divorce committee at page 597. Mr. Justice McRuer then went on to point out the complications when they are asked to review these matters of custody. They have to get in touch with the judge in the capital, in Toronto if the case is in Ontario, or elsewhere. He gave many illustrations of these difficulties.
The minister said something about not having to change this jurisdiction here in Ottawa, as the provinces can do this for themselves. I suggest that is not a good enough answer. If this parliament sets the jurisdiction in the superior court, I doubt very much if a province could do anything to shift it somewhere else. Let me read what Chief Justice McRuer told the committee- and the minister will find this at page 599 of the evidence, if he is interested. I do not

know whether he has even looked into this. He mentioned the case in the Supreme Court of Canada and the British Columbia case, although I have forgotten the name. Chief Justice McRuer said:
I would like to see in the first place a dominion act, in that it would be necessary for the dominion legislation to confer concurrent jurisdiction on the superior court and on the county court so far as Ontario is concerned. When you get to Quebec you do not have county courts, you only have the superior court there. In British Columbia they have been able to do this by provincial legislation. But I doubt very much if that could be done in Ontario, because the majority of the courts hinge around the history of the local judges of the supreme court, county court judges who are local judges of the supreme court.
Mr. Justice Judson's judgment would probably go the whole way and Ontario could do it, but I think it is very dangerous. I think it ought to be done clearly by legislation of the dominion government, because 20 years from now the point might be raised that the divorce was not valid because the court did not have the jurisdiction in a case where inheritance or something of that sort was involved; you have to be very, very sure of your ground.
The chief justice was speaking here about the necessity of dominion legislation to clear up this question of the jurisdiction of county courts. The minister suggests we should let the provinces do this, but I ask him to listen to what the chief justice of this high court said. I would not be in the least surprised if the chief justice of this high court, with years of experience in this field, knew a little bit more than those presently advising the minister in this regard. I suggest we do not need to leave this matter in doubt.
