I have a very brief explanation, Mr. Chairman. I must say that in the very few instances where the government departed from the recommendations of the joint committee we did so only after great hesitation an consideration. In reply to the hon. member for Greenwood, who wants to know more about who advised me, I must say this is a cabinet decision. There are in the cabinet a great many lawyers who have had a lot of practical experience in the application of divorce law.
I do not think I need go beyond saying that this is a government decision, not a personal one. I must take exception to the phrase the hon. member for Greenwood used, to the effect that I swept lightly aside the question of cost. I am afraid the hon. member was swept aside by his own enthusiasm and lack of memory. I did explain that this question of cost was an important one, but, the government considered that the question of principle had to be dealt with first; and, in view of the fact that we were introducing divorce law that went way beyond any divorce law which had existed in Canada hitherto, we felt that this completely new concept of divorce, at least during the initial years, should be adjudicated by the high courts and not by the county courts.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The reason of substance is the one that was given in the report, "Putting Asunder". It is not here a question of distance so much
Divorce Law Reform
as one of substantive law. It is of such a nature that it should be decided by the high courts at least during the early years. This was the first step taken by the government in terms of logic. Then it said: What is the consequence of this on costs? We realized that the costs question was not solved in the same way if the matter went to the high courts as if it went to the county courts. But we felt, as I explained this afternoon and this evening, that the question of costs is one that can be dealt with in another way. If, for reason of principles, we felt it should go to the high court, we decided we should follow our principles and that the question of costs could be decided in other ways, such as by consultation, as suggested by the hon. member for Halifax.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether it would help the minister if, because of the logic of the cabinet to which he has referred, there were added at the end of the proposed amendment, "provided, further, that such judges of county or district courts may exercise concurrent jurisdiction in any province upon the request of the lieutenant governor in council of that province"-in other words, take in the unanimous recommendation of the committee and make it a request of the province? I think this is frightfully important. We have had two expressions of opinion, plus the minister's response, but I have three other facts which I think must be injected into the debate.
This matter is really at the heart of, or is one of the real pedestals of divorce reform. The question has been asked whether it would mean a diminution of costs or less expense to the petitioner if there were county court jurisdiction in this matter. I think in honesty I would have to say, as a Nova Scotian lawyer, that we already have such differences in jurisdiction that the difference in cost is not a compelling factor; there would be less expense in county court, but not enough to justify the step that is being taken. However, I must point out to the committee that of some 470 divorce cases tried in Nova Scotian courts in the year 1966, there were 200 tried by county court judges exercising jurisdiction in the court for divorce and matrimonial causes, or the supreme court as it would be familiarly known here. That is almost 50 per cent of the cases.
So what is the logic of the cabinet decision going to do, if the minister does not accept the amendment? This logic would mean that for the next couple of years we will have

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
amendments to the Judges Act every year so that an extra couple of judges could be appointed in Ontario, British Columbia, etc., because the burden would simply become greater on the supreme court judges. We know, if I may use the word, that a conservative estimate of the number of divorce cases in Canada is now around the 9,000 mark per year and that this number will double at least for the next couple of years, throwing a burden on the courts that will be extraordinarily difficult to meet.
In Nova Scotia, even with the judges of the supreme court, and 11 of the 12 county court judges working on divorce cases, it will mean a tremendous load for them. But for other provinces where the county or district courts have no say at all, I would say the burden would become insuperable.
There is the point about readier access to judges. I talked to a lawyer in Truro, Nova Scotia, tonight. Truro is 60 miles from Halifax. Lawyers and their clients, one would think, could drive from Truro to Halifax to have their cases tried. But this lawyer said: Would you impress upon the House of Commons the fact that having our county court judges deal with divorce cases in Truro is, even though it is close to Halifax, a tremendous boon to parties because they would have to wait for a circuit judge to come to Truro or go to Halifax at some convenient time. When dealing with mileage and people losing half a day or a day's pay in order to be a witness, you are dealing with factors that are in my opinion pretty considerable. This is another reason why the county court approach commends itself.
Others have mentioned this matter but I think it should be banged home over and over again, as I did on second reading. The very first time I saw the bill it struck me as extraordinary that under clause 8 the judge must lean over and face the petitioner, respondent or both and say: Is there any chance that you can come together and give up seeking this divorce? One of them might say yes, and the dear old soul would then say: We will postpone this hearing for 14 days to give you a chance of reconciliation. And off he goes. As has been pointed out, he goes on circuit and it may take years and years to catch up with him.
What will be the effect of this provision? As a lawyer I have a duty imposed on me, when people come into my office, to say: Is there any hope that this marriage can be saved? I am sure other lawyers do this as

well. Under another clause of the bill you are supposed to give them certain advice. There will come a point early in the proceedings when the lawyer will have to say: "Madam petitioner, the judge will ask you whether there is any hope of reconciliation. I can advise you, my client, that if you say yes at that point your case will have gone for at least 14 days and you may never catch up with it again, or at least for months and months or years and years.
These are pretty considerable factors. I do not care what happened in 1912 in the Gorell committee. There was a different form of legal values then. We are talking of the here and now, and the unanimous recommendation of a divorce committee of both houses of parliament. If we are really serious about cutting costs for people, the amendment of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, commendable as it is and as much as I support it, will not be enough; we should have the guts to get down to a better administrative, more workable approach.
In any event, Mr. Chairman, let us deal with the here and now and arrive at the most practical measure possible. I suggest to the minister that if he does not like the amendment of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka perhaps he would consider it with these extras added:
Provided, further, that such judges of county or district courts may exercise concurrent jurisdiction in any province upon the request of the lieutenant governor in council of that province.
I so move, Mr. Chairman.

I will not have very much to say about this bill, Mr. Chairman, because, as will be understood, I am not deeply exercised about the widening of civil grounds for divorce. But I do suggest to the minister that he should carefully consider the amendment moved by the hon. member for Carleton, because what does concern me about this bill is the potentially great increase in cases that will come before our courts. I believe that what the Minister of Justice should consider is whether he will find that, having passed this bill, there should occur a log jam in the superior courts of this country.
I am seriously concerned that this may be the case, and therefore I commend to the minister the consideration of this amendment which gives to the lieutenant governor of a province or the territorial council the opportunity, if they find the superior courts becoming over-burdened with petitions for divorce, to petition the governor in council of Canada to relieve against that situation.

Mr. Chairman, I am not a lawyer and therefore I am not familiar with all the ramifications the Minister of Justice has indicated are involved in the consideration of this principle. It seems to me the proposition is a fairly simple one. We are going to have a backlog of cases as the previous speaker mentioned. The Canadian Bar Association says 500,000 people are involved, and this may represent 250,000 cases being brought before the courts in the next ten years. This will probably be equal to the

number of cases being heard by the courts previously. The minister raised an objection which in my opinion indicated that a number of judges of the country courts have been appointed who are incompetent, perhaps a far larger number than we are aware. This of course indicates that the patronage system we use to appoint judges is not a good one. I believe this is the only reason the minister has given for his objection to this procedure.
The minister said the decision with regard to giving jurisdiction to superior courts was a cabinet decision. I am sure they did not say they had to limit it to superior courts. No doubt the cabinet did say they would have to put these matters into courts where they would not get out of hand. I believe this statement illustrates the incompetence of county and district courts. This may be true, and if it is, then the 250,000 litigants who will be involved in divorce matters should not be foisted off on these lower courts.
The next matter of concern, of course, is costs. Then, too, on sundry occasions lawyers are always willing to bandy about that old phrase, "Justice delayed is justice denied". I know from my own limited experience there are cases now coming before the Supreme Court of Ontario which date back two years and which have not been heard as yet. If you ask about these cases you are told the judge has not had time to reach them. If you write the judge, he says the case was not on his docket and therefore the lawyer is to blame. If you ask the bar association they will say, "A plague on both your houses". The person making the inquiry is never sure who is to blame. He changes lawyers, tries again and the delay is continued.
I believe the minister should have a better argument than saying to the people of Canada or to members of parliament that this act is going to be so difficult to administer that only superior courts of the provinces are going to be able to handle it. We are not going to be faced with so many new divorce actions; but there have been many divorce actions pending the passage of this legislation. I am surprised at members on the other side. These are the members who stood up and said, "Let us not rush things", when this subject was before us two or three years ago. They should decide not to be sheep, and should take unto themselves the right which the Prime Minister gave on other occasions when moral matters were involved. This is a moral matter. Many people are waiting for relief from situations which developed

through no fault of their own, and this legislation will grant them some relief. It seems to me we have an obligation to see that they get their case before the courts as soon as possible, with as little cost as possible.
I am sure the minister is not prepared to come back to parliament and ask us to double the number of supreme court judges in any province. I suggest, too, that no negotiations take place in the back room between the minister and the attorney general of a province. We should decide here to give jurisdiction to county and district courts. Surely we will be able to make our legislation and regulations simple enough that even some of these judges who may be incompetent will be able to understand them. If we cannot, then this is a sad reflection on the type of judiciary we have at the junior level, and who appear before John Q. Public at all times. They should be able to understand what appears to me to be a fairly simply bill. We have to decide what the grounds of divorce are and what the regulations will be, but I do not think it is stretching the imagination too far to suggest that most county and district court judges are competent to handle the provisions of a simple bill.

Mr. Chairman, I introduced an amendment to clause 3. I will not discuss it at great length, but it deals with the basic question of the principle that is before the house.
The amendment that I now propose would base the law of divorce on the marriage breakdown approach. I spoke about this on the resolution stage and on second reading. Several members in the house, including the hon. members for Peace River, Royal, Parry Sound-Muskoka and others have also spoken about this.
I know that the minister will not accept my amendment. Quite frankly, I do not see how he could accept it because he has argued vigorously and at length that he is not prepared to do so. Nevertheless I propose to put this amendment before the committee in order that the principles that are involved may be made clear.
The principle is this. In the view of some of us it is necessary to change the whole approach to divorce. Divorce ought to be based not on a procedure of accusation, not on a determination of which of the parties is guilty or innocent, but on a finding of whether the marriage is dead. This is the basic principle I wish to make clear.
The minister spoke about this matter and said, that, although it might be a nice idea, it was totally impracticable. I do not agree with him; I think it is perfectly practicable. The Mortimer commission, according to the archbishop's committee, spoke about the pure form of breakdown. The minister said that that would have no application under this bill. He said that if we accepted the pure
Divorce Law Reform
form of breakdown we should become involved in an inquisitorial form of procedure. What I propose in my amendment is the following. I would move:
That section 3 of the bill C-187 be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
(1)	A petition for divorce may be presented to a court by a husband or wife on the ground that a marriage has irretrievably broken down and that there is no reasonable likelihood of reconciliation.
That is the basic amendment that I propose. It substitutes the one matter of marriage breakdown for all the concepts of matrimonial fault, all the rigmarole of collusion, connivance, condonation and the phony adultery trials. That is all the courts would need to determine. The minister said, after quoting the British report, that adopting the marriage breakdown concept would entail an inquisition into a marriage, in every case. I recognize that problem and for that reason I include subclause 2, as follows:
(2)	Where the parties have lived separate and apart for a period of not less than three years, then it shall be prima facie presumed that the marriage has irretrievably broken down and that there is no reasonable likelihood of reconciliation.
The minister might say that that is not the pure form of breakdown. I am not interested in purity; I am interested in something that will work. At the end of a lenghty separation-I do not care whether it is three years or five years, or whatever the period is-the court would be entitled to presume the breakdown of the marriage.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
There would then, under those circumstances, be no need for lengthy inquests or difficult inquiries. As a matter of fact it might not be much more difficult than it is today to go through these hotel and motel trials that we have had. With respect to the third subclause in my amendment, it reads:
(3)	The court may refuse to grant a decree of dissolution of the marriage if it is satisfied that to grant a decree might prove unduly harsh and repressive to the respondent.
The reason I include that is that it is possible to conceive of a case in which a person has behaved very badly and that person might seek a divorce, but the courts might think it a hardship on the wife to grant the divorce. Therefore Mr. Chairman, I will move that clause 3 be amended, and my amendment be substituted for it. If this amendment were adopted-and I am not over optimistic that I can suddenly persuade the solid phalanxes of the government to agree with me at this

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
stage of the day-then clauses 4, 7, 8 and 9 of the bill would not be necessary.
This is a new concept, a concept supported by the churches, a concept put before our committee and which we think makes sense. It bypasses the old method of doing things. It bypasses 30 years of English experience of doing things, and I suggest puts the matter on a more fruitful and sounder basis. The object of divorce legislation should be to provide that where the marriage tie no longer represents a reality, where the marriage is completely dead, and when it no longer serves the purpose of marriage, which is the life-long living together of a man and a woman, then the law shall determine that the marriage is at an end. It has been suggested that I should read this amendment again, Mr. Chairman. I am perfectly willing to do so. I shall read it in English and perhaps you, Mr. Chairman, might read it in French. I move:
That section 3 of Bill C-187 be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"3. (1) A petition for divorce may be presented to a court by a husband or wife on the ground that a marriage has irretrievably broken down and that there is no reasonable likelihood of reconciliation.
(2)	Where the parties have lived separate and apart for a period of not less than three years, then it shall be prima facie presumed that the marriage has irretrievably broken down and that there is no reasonable likelihood of reconciliation.
(3)	The court may refuse to grant a decree of dissolution of the marriage if it is satisfied that to grant a decree might prove unduly harsh and repressive to the respondent."
As I have mentioned, if this amendment were adopted it would also replace clauses 4, 7, 8 and 9 of the bill.

Many jurisdictions have long since amended their divorce legislation. I hoped that I would have been part of a parliament that could have been a real pioneer in the matter of the reform of divorce laws. Perhaps parliament, to quote a well known statesman, is too timid to excite the daring.
The Montreal Star in an editorial on December 11 had this to say about the present bill, under the heading "Divorce Compromise":
Where the bill falls short of social need is in its attempt to define marriage breakdown, to set limits within which a broken marriage must fall before a court can say that breakdown is irrevocable. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make this one point, so that it will be clear why I think this bill is incomplete and why I believe one idea of the marriage breakdown theory would be acceptable. Here we have in the bill under subclause (e) what in effect is a marriage breakdown clause. It merely provides for divorce if the parties have been living separate for three years. The report of the joint committee and the opinion of most people who are in favour of the marriage breakdown theory in Canada is to the effect that this must be hedged about by some safeguards, and that it is not good enough just to create a ground for divorce and call a marriage breakdown a cause for a divorce. This is not good enough.
The recommendation of the joint committee was that, in addition to what is in this bill, the court must find, before it can grant a divorce, first, that the marriage is permanently finished; second, that every reasonable effort at reconciliation has failed; third, that there is no likelihood of the situation improving in the future; fourth, that the question of due care and maintenance of the children is settled; fifth, that no public interest is affected and, finally, that no undue hardship on the other spouse will result.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
That is what the special joint committee recommended, and if the present bill had those safeguards and everything else was eliminated but clause 4 (l)(e), we would have a reasonably acceptable marriage breakdown

bill. What we have is a marriage breakdown ground without the safeguards. The safeguards are not there, and it is my opinion that what I propose, which is in essence contained in the amendment, should be included. If you are going to allow a divorce merely after three years separation the least you can do is make sure you have a perfectly valid case, that the marriage is at an end, that efforts have been made to restore it and every other provision has been satisfied in favour of separating two people. This is what I say is wrong with this bill and why I am in favour of a limited marriage breakdown proposal.
The minister did, as he stated in his own words, go a long way toward what I consider the ground of marriage breakdown. In fact, I think he went so far he could have eliminated the rest of his bill and left this one provision in, and have a good marriage breakdown bill by adding the safeguards I would put in.

Mr. Chairman, 1 do not want unduly to delay the passage of this bill in the committee, and I did not enter the debate on second reading for that reason, but I should like as briefly as possible to put on the record my feelings about hon. members' suggestions. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka very logically brought out in respect of the marriage breakdown concept the very reasons for my opposition to it.
I know it has been said in the house and reported in the press that this concept that was placed before the committee, of which I did not have the honour to be a member, was a modern, progressive theory of divorce reform that we should adopt, namely the theory of marriage breakdown. The amendment of the hon. member for Greenwood that is before the committee is to strike out all the specific causes and all the marital offence clauses and simply substitute the concept of marriage breakdown.
The reason I oppose this amendment is that I think it would make divorce a great deal harder to obtain in this country than will be the case under the bill as it now stands. It seems to me that the amendment before us could run the risk of leading to a situation where it would be almost impossible to prove before a judge that the marriage had in fact broken down.
The requirements of proof under the amendment are that the marriage has irretrievably broken down and there is no reasonable likelihood of reconciliation. I can imagine judges in my own jurisdiction, and without making any invidious references at
Divorce Law Reform
all I can well imagine judges in the province of Quebec, for example, before whom it would be virtually impossible for petitioners to prove that the marriage had irretrievably broken down and that there was no reasonable likelihood of reconciling the parties.
It seems to me that petitioners before the courts have a right to divorce on the grounds enumerated in clause 3, and they should not have to prove to the court that the marriage had broken down because one of those offences has been committed and there was no chance of reconciling it. I believe that if one spouse has committed adultery, the other spouse has the right, as a matter of freedom of choice, to decide whether he or she should go to court and ask for a dissolution of the marriage. It seems to me that if one spouse has committed bigamy, the other spouse should have the right to go before the courts and, after proving the first marriage, the second marriage and the identity of the parties, obtain a divorce on the ground of bigamy.
One could deal with all the specific grounds of clause 3 which the amendment seeks to strike out. In my view the people who are concerned, those who become involved in marital situations, should have the right to go to court and ask for a dissolution of their marriage on these grounds. To pass this amendment, and require them to go through the difficulty of proof that I can envisage in the amendment, would make it extremely difficult in some jurisdictions to obtain a divorce and would, I suggest, lead to an extremely costly procedure for the parties involved.
A moment ago I mentioned the question of bigamy. It seems to me that if someone has the right to a divorce or dissolution of his or her marriage on the ground of bigamy, it is a fairly simple procedure to prove the first and second marriages and the identities of the parties involved. But if this amendment were accepted, a person whose spouse had committed adultery would have to go to court and prove something far more difficult, first that the marriage had irretrievably broken down, and second that there was no reasonable likelihood of reconciliation.
I believe that there are in this country judges who, in spite of the fact that one's spouse had committed bigamy, would still say: You should go to a couple of psychiatrists and see if you cannot work out your problems and keep this marriage alive.

I knew I would get applause for that statement. However, I do want to comment on what was said by the hon. member for Kamloops. I am not sure I have his exact words but I think he said that the concept of marriage breakdown would strike at the sanctity of marriage. I want to take exception to that point of view. I may be wrong, and we are all entitled to our own opinion on this matter, but the fact of the matter is that this proposal was put before the divorce committee first of all by the United Church, second it was fully supported by the Anglican Church of Canada, and third, it is in line with the report made by a group of churchmen appointed by the Archbishop of Canterbury. The point they made is that the breakdown theory is more consonant with what I would call a Christian or a religious concept of marriage. I agree that we in parliament must not necessarily try, and the church does not ask us, to enforce a view of marriage which is consistent with the religious view.
The church recognizes that we are legislating for the community as a whole, but they made it very clear that in their view a secular divorce law based upon breakdown would do more honour to the principle of marriage as a lifelong union than would a divorce law based upon the so-called matrimonial misconduct.
This, in a sense, meets what the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has said. He is perfectly right, the marriage breakdown concept would make it harder for some people to get a divorce. It would certainly mean that perhaps in cases of a casual act of adultery the courts would have to inquire whether or not there is a possibility of reconciliation. So in some cases it might narrow the opportunity for obtaining a divorce. On the other hand it would broaden the opportunity for obtaining a divorce to include all other cases in which the marriage in fact was found to be dead and there was no likelihood of the parties getting together. So in some respects this

concept narrows down the possibility of obtaining a divorce and in other respects it broadens it, but it is a new and a different concept.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a few words on this matter as an Anglican who differs from my friend from Greenwood and also from the Rev. E. S. Reed, Bishop of Ottawa, and other Anglicans who presented evidence before the committee. I can tell these hon. gentlemen that they did not represent many Anglicans in this country when they made their representations before the committee, although I am sure they made them in good faith and with the best intentions.
I should like to read briefly from page 119 of the report dealing with grounds for divorce. It reads as follows:
The commission points out that not only would trial procedure be more painful to the parties, hut it would be considerably more extensive in the time and space it would occupy. If all cases were to be inquired into, trials would inevitably be longer. The vast majority of cases at present are undefended and therefore can be dealt with both swiftly and without complications. The proposed system would necessitate more courts, more judges, and, most essential, the new procedure would require large numbers of trained investigators and social workers to assist the court. All this would be extremely expensive and would have to be paid for largely by the taxpayer, although it would no doubt be reflected in higher cost of divorce to the parties as well. Far from making divorces simpler and cheaper, it might well have the opposite effect.
I want to say in this connection that I have had some discussions with members of the committee and members of the other place who are very well versed on this problem, because I was somewhat concerned about various proposals put forward to establish the breakdown of marriage as the only ground for divorce.
As I said before, I talked to some members of the committee and some members of the other place who are well informed on the subject. They told me that if this section were implemented a certain amount of snooping would be involved into the private affairs of individuals. I must say I take a very dim view of any procedure that would entail this sort of thing. I base my stand on an experience I had some years ago, and I am going to cite that experience.
A lady I knew of impeccable character, whose husband had left her, was in receipt of relief owing to her unfortunate circumstances. The social welfare worker, who at that time had no training, called on the
December 18, 1967

neighbours to enquire if this lady was living a good moral life. Two or three of the ladies informed her they had seen a man's laundry on the clothesline. The lady from the welfare agency searched the house and found a box of man's laundry. This laundry had been done by the lady out of the goodness of her heart for an old gentleman who was in poor circumstances. As a result of this snooping, the lady in question was promptly denied her welfare payments. The whole village, who knew the lady very well, was in an uproar and she finally got her welfare payments back because of the indignation of many good Anglicans and other church people in the district.
I was told by these gentlemen in the other place that if we have the breakdown theory incorporated in the bill, as suggested by some members on this side of the house,-and I fully appreciate their sincerity,-it would involve some snooping on the part of social welfare workers, probably at the corner grocery store, to find out how the people were getting on together. If I am incorrect in my understanding, I should like the minister to explain the meaning of this amendment before we conclude debate on this section. I am one who is very concerned about that sort of thing in every aspect of life because I believe in the rights of the individual.
In conclusion, I want to say a word or two about the concluding paragraph of this report which appears on page 122. It reads:
The real problem with this simplified version of the marriage breakdown theory is an extremely basic one. How long a period of separation should be required before a husband or wife can ask the courts for a divorce? The witnesses proposing the inclusion of separation as a grounds for divorce in some system or another, have suggested various periods of time ranging from two to seven years. Similarly, the Mortimer group in England thought three years; the members of the English Royal Commission on Marriage and Divorce (1951-1955) believed seven years to be a reasonable time. If the period chosen is too short, the parties might rush into a divorce without having time to recover from either a violent matrimonial quarrel or a passing affair or infatuation. Nor might they have time to consider whether the difficulties in their marriage were capable of solution.
On the other hand, if the period is a relatively long one, say three years, what becomes of those who presently can obtain divorces on the ground of outrageous conduct by their spouse? Must they have to wait three years? It seems unlikely that a period could be agreed that would render justice to all parties in both categories. Therefore, it does not seem possible that breakdown could constitute the sole and comprehensive ground.
I accept that statement.
If the period of separation is to be more than six months, then it can only offer a practical
Divorce Law Reform
solution if it is coupled with other grounds which would provide more rapid relief. This is not to reject marriage breakdown ideas completely. Far from it. The introduction of it through the ground of separation is discussed in the following section of the report.
I just want to say there is no question but that the introduction of this bill is a great step forward toward the curing of growing social difficulties in Canada. We give the minister credit for that. I suggest we should get experience from the application of this bill and as a result of that experience on the part of the federal and provincial governments as well as the courts, we can come to some conclusions which would make it easier to amend this act, with all respect for the marriage ties.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Amendment (Mr. Brewin) negatived: Yeas, 15; nays, 73.

The minister shakes his head. I do not know how much practice he has had with regard to this kind of matter, but there are cases of persons entering into a form of marriage believing themselves free to do so, and there have been no actual sexual relations. This is not the ground in paragraph (c); its provisions relate to a person who has gone through a form of marriage with another person whether entitled to do so or not.
I wonder why this ground of divorce is being introduced. This afternoon I asked the minister why incurable insanity was not included as a ground and I received no answer. Grounds for less serious matters are included in the bill. For instance where a person has become an alcoholic or a drug addict for a period of

December 18. 1967

three years and there is no reasonable expectation that he will be rehabilitated within the reasonably foreseeable future, relief is granted.
Again, I put strictures on such types of interpretation. Under this legislation a person who is married to an alcoholic, for whom in the reasonably foreseeable future there is no cure, is granted relief. speechtext: With respect to the first point, which has to do with clause 3(c), the form of marriage. As the hon. member assumed, that clause was included in order to facilitate proof of this offence. Take the case where a husband has left the country and has gone to live in some other country with some other person.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: Tibet, say.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: If this clause were not included the petitioner would have to go to the expense, trouble and difficulty of proving an adulterous relationship with the corespondent. As a result of the inclusion of this clause the petitioner need only bring some kind of certificate to show that the respondent has gone through a form of marriage. The difficulties with respect to proof are largely avoided.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask a question. When the cabinet considered the wording "has gone through a form of marriage" did it intend that that form of marriage should be a form of marriage that is recognized by Canadian law?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
I should not give away secrets of cabinet. Let it suffice to say that "form of marriage" was used precisely to indicate that it could be a kind of marriage ceremony or relationship which is not provided for under our law, but which corresponds to our general concept of marriage.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
There could be any type of marriage which is recognized in another country, which would have the effect of a bigamist relationship. But once again it is in order to avoid

the proof of adultery that we use this expression "form of marriage" as attested by whatever documentary evidence is admissible in our courts, as to the existence of some marital relationship elsewhere.
On the other point of incurable insanity, I can only indicate to the hon. member for Edmonton West that this particular case would be solved by clause 4(e)(i). If the petitioner was not living separate and apart for three years from the person who is incurably insane, or who indeed is inflicted with any incurable disease-it could be physical as well as mental-we are asking parliament to assume he did not want a divorce.
A husband or wife, out of Christian charity and out of love for their spouse, may decide to live with the afflicted or diseased partner. As a matter of fact I hope this will happen in a great number of cases and that the parties will not be encouraged to separate under this legislation, merely because we permit a divorce at the end of three years. We are assuming that a great many people will continue to live with their spouses despite the fact that their spouses are ill. But we are saying in this bill that if one of the parties decides not to live with the other sick party, and has not done so for three years, then we take this as evidence of marriage breakdown.
Therefore you have the three year test here, the same as in the narcotic or alcholic ease, the difference being that in one case they do not have to live separate and apart, while in the sickness case they would have to live separate and apart. The problem raised by the hon. member is met in this way. I think the government showed some distaste for spelling out the sickness case, lest it appear to assume that the parties would be deciding to separate merely because one of them was incurably ill. But it is certain if that is the case, and they do decide to separate, their divorce will become possible under clause 4(e)(i).

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I know that most marriage ceremonies include the words, as mentioned by my learned colleague from Queens, "in sickness and in health until death do us part," but I am just wondering whether it is quite right, if we are going to go to this extent in opening up the grounds for divorce, that the person who is married to an individual who becomes violently and incurably insane has to wait for three years under the provisions of clause 4(e)(i), as the minister has indicated. What is the rationale
December 18, 1967

in making that person wait for three years? After all, it is not the will of the parties which separates them. It is the state which takes the person who is incurably insane and puts him in a mental hospital or asylum. That is a forcible living apart caused by illness, but with the sanction of the state. In those circumstances what would justify the waiting period of three years? The waiting period of three years with regard to the alcoholic and drug addict does not specify that they shall have lived apart for that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: There is no magic in the three years. We have taken this test, and I think it is a rather conservative one, as indicative of a decision of the parties to seek divorce. If one looks at the ground for divorce under the English law he will find that it is unsound mind or continuously under care for five years. In Australia it is unsound mind and unlikely to recover, and has been confined for a period in the aggregate of five years. In New Zealand it is unsound mind for an aggregate of seven years out of the previous ten. These are not magic figures. We are using a rather liberal figure of three. I suppose I have no explanation other than to say that we want to be a little more liberal than some of these other countries. I have other examples from other countries, but I do not wish to take up the time of the house now.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee which had something to do with the drafting of clause 3 (c) in its original form, I might say that some of us were aware of cases before parliament involving, for example, a Nevada type of divorce which the party who remained in Canada found could not be recognized here. This party did not have to prove that the divorce had gone through, but had to prove that the other person had been involved in adultery or sexual intercourse with another person. This meant that the party was involved in the old detective situation. This meant that hundreds of dollars were involved in having to fly detectives to Nevada, or wherever the person had wound up. This might add $1,000 or more to the cost of the petition. We thought it was high time that a situation of that kind was cured. In today's world, especially when dealing with 50 different types of divorce jurisdictions in the U.S.A. alone, we thought it was high time something was done about this situation.

Clause agreed to.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, subclause (1) (d) of clause 4 intrigues me. It permits a divorce on the ground that the marriage has not been consummated. I confess I am one of those innocents who always believes there is no marriage unless it is consummated. How can you dissolve an unconsummated marriage on the ground of divorce? This is something which passes my understanding. I think the minister has nullity and annulment confused with divorce in this regard. I believe, as well, he has become involved in some difficulty in relation to recognition, domicile and other aspects relating to the matter of nullity versus divorce, or annulment versus divorce. I do not intend to raise the issue at this hour of the night or to pursue it to any extent, but from a legal concept I believe subclause (d) makes absolute nonsense of the law which hon. gentlemen in this house who have been trained in the law have learned at a variety of law schools.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.

Mr. Chairman, I think I can answer that briefly. If one looks further on in the bill at clause 26 (2) he will find that this repeals all other laws respecting divorce but that this repeal provision does not repeal the law to the extent that it constitutes authority for other matrimonial causes. This clause 4 (1) (d) is necessary to catch the so-called annulment cases or non-consummation cases which are not caught by the annulment clauses of existing legislation.
[DOT] (10:40 p.m.)
I will give one example. Under the civil code in the province of Quebec you can obtain an annulment for non-consummation when there are physical defects and so on, provided you demand it within a period of three years. If you do not, your right for annulment under the civil code is lost. This present provision would help people who had lost the right under the civil code. They could still act under this law, and that is the reason we have this type of change. While I am on my feet-

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext:
May I interpose a question here? I am wondering why we should try to relieve laches in this way where the provincial code imposes a penalty for laches with regard to bringing an action under voidable grounds? After all the marriage that is non-consummated is not void ab initio, it is merely voidable. The minister fully understands what we are talking about, even if some of

December 18, 1967
Divorce Law Reform
the technical legal terms escape other hon. members. Why in these particular instances should we include this one ground in respect of a voidable marriage? Why not include as well the legal incapacity to enter into a marriage which, of course, is a ground for annulment, and the other grounds? The rationale would be the same. I cannot see why we should cure with this bill those laches which are imposed by the Quebec civil code, if they are retained in respect of a time limit. We have this in other jurisdictions as well. Why are you relieving the situation in this respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: For the very simple reason that we are providing a double remedy for failure to consummate because of physical impotency, one remedy being annulment, and the other being divorce because of marriage breakdown. This does not apply to non-consummation because of wilful refusal. In the case of wilful refusal only the divorce remedy would apply. In the province of Quebec, for instance, you cannot get an annulment even within three years because of wilful refusal when obviously there is no physical impotency. Under this hypothesis if a person had never consummated the marriage and refused to do so for a period of three years the remedy of divorce would apply.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: I should like to support this amendment for a different reason. From what was said at the committee hearing and from my own experience in this regard, the part with reference to refusing to consummate the marriage relates to another problem which came to our attention. I refer to the example of a homosexual for reasons of convenience getting married and not consummating the marriage. This has happened in a number of cases and it is almost impossible under any circumstances to find a remedy in any period of time. It seems to me this will solve this problem, particularly if it means what I as a layman consider it to mean.

Paragraph (c) bothers me a little, Mr. Chairman. It provides that the marriage shall be deemed to have broken down if, for a period of not less than three years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition, the petitioner has had no knowledge of or information as to the whereabouts of the respondent, and so on. I am wondering whether, as a matter of precaution, it would not be advisable to insert in there that some reasonable effort must first have been made to acquire the knowledge.
This provision makes it unreasonably easy for a petitioner to go into court and simply say: I do not know where my spouse has been for the past three years. Having said that, the marriage is deemed to have broken down-

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: What about the last words of that paragraph?

The last words are
"throughout that period, has been unable to locate the respondent." I suggest that the petitioner should establish that he or she has made some reasonable effort to locate the other spouse. I suggest that words to the following effect should be inserted somewhere in the clause, "having first made reasonable efforts to acquire the knowledge", or,

"'having first made some reasonable effort to locate the other party."
An amendment of this sort would not seriously affect the bill. While we all agree that worthy cases should be given relief, I think some precaution must be taken to protect the marriage state and not make divorces too easy to obtain. I do not think this would be an unreasonable burden to place upon a petitioner, namely to show that he or she has made some reasonable effort to acquire knowledge as to where the other spouse has been, and that he or she has made some reasonable effort to locate the other spouse.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister how wedded he is to the three year period mentioned in clause 4 (e). It seems to me that one year would be a sufficiently long period of time and would serve the purpose of protecting children not yet born at the time of separation. I wonder if the minister would accept an amendment for two years, which would be a compromise.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I repeat that there is no magic in this figure of three. It is the figure which has been suggested by the joint committee. Subclause (e) mentions three years, subclause (a) mentions two years where the spouse is in prison and subclause (d) mentions not less than one year in the case of non-consummation. Here again I can only say that we have not been unduly severe. In the British law the period for desertion is three years. Frankly, we are not wedded to this time period, but we have given consideration to the various periods possible and we thought that three years would be a good start. The hon. member realizes that if we were to change the three year period in this subclause, consequent changes would have to be made in the other subclauses.

-where the existence of any of the circumstances described in subsection 1 has been established, a 27053-352

permanent breakdown of the marriage by reason of those circumstances shall be deemed to have been established.
The minister is aware that there are presumptions in law which are rebuttable, and there are irrebuttable presumptions. That is to say there is a presumption which exists until it is disproved, or there is a presumption which cannot be disproved by evidence to the contrary. I wonder which form of presumption is referred to here. I call the minister's attention to the following words in subclause 9 (d):
-where a decree is sought under section 4, to refuse the decree if there is a reasonable expectation that cohabitation will occur or be resumed within a reasonably foreseeable period.
I would assume that subclause 2 creates an irrebuttable assumption that the marriage has broken down, but it might be useful to clarify this and I invite the minister to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this subclause is clearly a precautionary one. We are just stating that the court in certain circumstances must come to the conclusion that there is a breakdown. The law could have been written without this clause, but we wanted to make it clear that it was the obligation of the court in certain circumstances to reach the conclusion that there was a breakdown in the marriage. This does not prevent it from acting under other clauses. Once again this is perhaps an excess of zeal on the part of conscientious draftsmen, but I think the clause may be useful and is certainly not harmful.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING GROUNDS, JURISDICTION, JUDGES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question with regard to clause 4 (1) (a) (i) and (ii) in which the words "the respondent has been in prison for a period of not less than two years" appear. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to take any part whatever in the discussion of this divorce bill. However, since the house has seen fit to grant an extra hour to discuss it, there is a point or two which I

December 18. 1967
Divorce Law Reform,
want to comment upon. Now, clause 4 (1) Cb) reads:
.-the respondent has, for a period of not less than three years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition, been grossly addicted to alcohol or a narcotic, as defined in the Narcotic Control Act, and there is no reasonable expectation of the respondent's rehabilitation within a reasonably foreseeable period;
This is not the first time that this mundane parliament has discussed a moral question. Recently we were adjured and advised that people were beyond the pale if they did not spend the rest of their lives in reforming criminals. I presume a person who is considered to be grossly addicted to alcohol or a narcotic must be considered a criminal since he must have had at least one conviction if not more registered against him.
In view of the great moral lectures that were read to us in the very recent past, I should like to quote from a speech delivered by Sir Winston Churchill in the British House of Commons some years ago when he was Home Secretary:
The mood and temper of the public with regard to the treatment of crime and criminals is one of the most unfailing tests of the civilization of any country. A calm dispassionate recognition of the rights of the accused, and even of the convicted criminal against the state; a constant heart-searching by all charged with the duty of punishment; a desire and an eagerness to rehabilitate ...; tireless efforts toward the discovery of creative and regenerate processes; unfailing faith that there is a treasure, if you can find it, in the heart of every man. These are the symbols which . .. mark and measure the stored-up strength of a nation ... proof of the living virtue in it.
Then, a few years ago, in an article in the New Statesman, Anthony Storr made the following statement:
To condemn him as inhuman is to fall into the trap of treating him as he treated his victims; as a thing, not a person, a thing on whom we can let loose our own sadistic impulses, not a fellow creature who might, even yet, be redeemed.
As the South African writer Alan Paton once wrote:
-but to punish and not to restore, that is the greatest of all offences.
A few weeks ago, in discussing one aspect of moral law, we were asked to spend the rest of our lives reforming certain people. In this bill, introduced by the same cabinet, we are told to spend three years and at the end of three years we are to come to the conclusion that there is no hope for this criminal.
Therefore he can be deprived of his spouse. If we are going to read moral lectures to the public of Canada to the effect that they must spend the rest of their lives reforming criminals, why should they not spend the rest of their lives reforming those people addicted to narcotics or drink as specified in this bill?
This bill imposes a three year limit, and at the end of three years we will show the criminal what we will do to him. We are going to deprive him of his spouse. I was brought up on the old principle that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. I do not like duplicity. I do not like hearing people use an argument one day to the effect that we must spend the rest of our lives reforming those who are unreformable, and then the next day be presented with a bill to the effect that at the end of three years we conclude there is no reasonable expectation for rehabilitation of a person within a reasonably foreseeable period. In so far as one type of person is concerned, we spend eight years, ten months and one day reforming him, but we are told that after three years we can come to the conclusion there is no reasonable expectation for rehabilitation of this other type of person within the foreseeable future.
